Cultivation and Processing of Common Anemarrhena Rhizome (Zhi Mu)
Source
The rhizome of the plant Anemarrhena asphodeloides of the Liliaceae family. It is dug in spring and autumn, old leaves and fibrous roots are removed, soil shaken off, and sun-dried or oven-dried to produce the raw hairy rhizome. If the fresh rhizome is peeled of its outer skin and then sun-dried, it becomes the fleshy Common Anemarrhena Rhizome.
Taste and Nature
Bitter in taste; cold in nature
Processing
1. Common Anemarrhena Rhizome (Zhi Mu): select and clean impurities, wash with water, lift out, moisten and soften, slice and sun-dry.
2. Salt-processed Common Anemarrhena Rhizome (Salt Zhi Mu): take slices of Zhi Mu, place in a pan and lightly stir-fry over low heat, spray with saline solution, fry until dry and remove to cool. (For every 100 jin of Zhi Mu slices, use 2 jin 8 liang of salt with an appropriate amount of boiled water to dissolve); first finely rasp on a locust-wood plank, dry by roasting, pound in a wooden mortar, avoid contact with iron utensils; select the plump, moist, inner-white pieces, remove hairs and cut; if the purpose is to guide fire upward use wine to soak and then roast dry, if to guide downward use saline water to moisten and roast.
Description
(1) Raw hairy Common Anemarrhena Rhizome
The rhizome is flattened, cylindrical and long-strip shaped, slightly curved, occasionally branched, 3–15 cm long, 0.8–1.5 cm in diameter. One end has pale yellow stem-leaf scars, commonly called the “gold-wrapped head.” The surface is yellow-brown to brown, with a groove on the upper side and closely arranged annular nodes, densely covered on the nodes with yellow-brown remaining leaf bases; the lower side is slightly convex, with longitudinal wrinkles and pitted root scars or fibrous root scars and residual stems. Texture hard and breaks easily. The fracture surface is yellow-white and granular. Aroma slight, taste slightly sweet with slight bitterness, chewed it is somewhat mucilaginous.
(2) Fleshy Common Anemarrhena Rhizome
Most of the outer skin has been removed; the surface is yellow-white, with occasional remaining hair-like leaf stems and pitted root scars. The best pieces are thick strips, hard in texture, and with a white-yellow fracture surface.
Effects of Common Anemarrhena Rhizome
Functions and Indications
The rhizome of the plant Anemarrhena asphodeloides of the Liliaceae family.
Treats vexing heat and excessive thirst, steaming bone disorder and consumptive heat, lung-heat cough, dry and hard stools, and difficult urination.
Channels Entered
Lung channel; Stomach channel; Kidney channel
Main Indications
Nourishes yin and reduces fire, moistens dryness and lubricates the intestines. Treats vexing heat and excessive thirst, steaming bone disorder and consumptive heat, lung-heat cough, dry and hard stools, and difficult urination.
Used for warm-heat diseases where pathogenic heat is exuberant, high fever, vexing thirst, surging-large pulse and other excess heat patterns of the lung and stomach. Zhi Mu clears heat, drains fire and relieves vexation. It acts synergistically with Gypsum Fibrosum (Shi Gao), for example in Bai Hu Tang.
Used for lung-heat coughs or yin-deficiency dry cough with scanty sputum. This herb clears and drains lung heat and nourishes yin to moisten the lungs; it is often combined with Fritillaria Bulb (Bei Mu) to clear the lungs, transform phlegm and stop cough, as in Er Mu San.
Used for yin deficiency with blazing fire, and signs from lung and kidney deficiency such as steaming of the bones, tidal fever, night sweats, and vexation. Zhi Mu nourishes yin and reduces fire. It is often paired with Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai) and included in yin-nourishing prescriptions, such as Zhi Bai Di Huang Wan.
Used for yin-deficiency diabetes-type thirst with signs of excessive thirst, copious drinking and frequent urination. This herb nourishes yin, moistens dryness, generates fluids and relieves thirst. Combined with Trichosanthes Root (Tian Hua Fen), Schisandra Fruit (Wu Wei Zi), etc., it enhances effects, as in Yu Ye Tang.
Dosage and Administration
Internal use: decocted, 6–12 g, or used in pills or powders.
To clear heat and drain fire, nourish yin and moisten dryness it is best used raw; to enter the kidney to reduce fire and nourish yin use salt-processed Zhi Mu.
Contraindications and Cautions
Contraindicated in spleen and stomach cold deficiency with loose stools.
1. Bie Lu: Excessive dosage causes diarrhea.
2. Introduction to Medicine: For cold cough in the lung, kidney qi collapse, or cases without heat with a weak inch pulse, avoid use.
3. Ben Cao Jing Shu: Contraindicated in impotence with premature ejaculation or easy loss of erection, diarrhea from spleen weakness, indigestion, stomach deficiency with poor appetite, kidney deficiency with watery diarrhea, etc.
4. Ben Jing Feng Yuan: Avoid when there is an unresolved exterior syndrome, in dysentery with dry thirst. If people with spleen-stomach deficiency and heat mistakenly take it, it causes diarrhea and reduces appetite, thus it is a great taboo in deficiency damage.
Formulas Using Common Anemarrhena Rhizome
1) For cold damage with internal excess heat, dry mouth and teeth, vexing thirst causing drinking, dim vision and dry lips: Zhi Mu 5 qian, Gypsum Fibrosum (Shi Gao) 3 qian, Ophiopogon (Mai Dong) 2 qian, Licorice (Gan Cao) 1 qian, Ginseng (Ren Shen) 8 qian. Decoct and take. (Shang Han Yun Yao)
2) For warm malaria with strong fever and inability to eat: Zhi Mu, Turtle Shell (Bie Jia) (roasted), Di Gu Pi, each 3 liang; Changshan 2 liang; bamboo leaf (Dan Zhu Ye) (sliced) one sheng; Gypsum Fibrosum (Shi Gao) 4 liang (crushed). Cut the six ingredients, take 7 sheng of water, boil down to 2 sheng 5 he, remove dregs, divide into three doses. Avoid garlic, pork, amaranth greens, raw scallion and raw lettuce. (Yan Nian Fang: Zhi Mu Bie Jia Tang)
3) For heat attacking causing vertigo and fainting with collapse, loss of consciousness, possibly urinary incontinence, then sweating with lightness returning, right guan pulse thin and scattered, spleen yin insufficiency: Zhi Mu, Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai), Astragalus Root (Huang Qi), Angelica Root (Dang Gui) body. Decoct and take. (Zheng Yin Mai Zhi: Zhi Bai Bu Xue Tang)
4) For diabetes-type thirst: fresh Chinese Yam (Shan Yao) 1 liang, fresh Astragalus Root (Huang Qi) 5 qian, Zhi Mu 6 qian, Chicken Gizzard Membrane (Ji Nei Jin) (pounded fine) 2 qian, Kudzu Root (Ge Gen) 1 qian 5 fen, Schisandra Fruit (Wu Wei Zi) 3 qian, Trichosanthes Root (Tian Hua Fen) 3 qian. Decoct and take. (Yi Xue Zhong Zhong Can Xi Lu: Yu Ye Tang)
5) For qi-deficiency consumptive wasting, sallow complexion and emaciation, timid qi and scattered spirit, lassitude of movement, morning cough and vexation with afternoon coolness, rapid pulse with heat: Zhi Mu 3 qian, Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai) 3 qian, Ginseng (Ren Shen) 2 qian, Ophiopogon (Mai Dong) 5 qian, aged Citrus Peel (Chen Pi) 1 qian, Licorice (Gan Cao) 5 fen. Decoct and take. (Zheng Yin Mai Zhi: Zhi Bai Shen Dong Yin)
6) For lung-consumption with real heat, facial bitterness and swelling, cough with rapid panting, vexing heat and flushed cheeks, many bone and joint pains, alternating chills and fever: Zhi Mu, Fritillaria Bulb (Chuan Bei Mu) (remove core membrane), Apricot Kernel (Ku Xing Ren) (peeled tip removed and stir-fried), Lepidium Seed (Ting Li Zi) (lightly stir-fried), Pinellia Rhizome (Ban Xia) (soak seven times in decoction), Gentiana (Qin Jiao) (remove reed), Immature Tangerine Peel (Ju Hong) each one liang, Licorice (Gan Cao) (roasted) half liang. Cut finely, each dose four qian, water half a cup, five slices of ginger, decoct to eight tenths, remove dregs and take warm, not restricted by time. (Ji Sheng Fang: Er Mu Tang)
7) For lung injured by dryness with cough and rebellious qi: Zhi Mu, Gypsum Fibrosum (Shi Gao), Platycodon Root (Jie Geng), Licorice (Gan Cao), Di Gu Pi. Decoct and take. (Zheng Yin Mai Zhi: Zhi Mu Gan Jie Tang)
8) For pregnancy agitation with fetal unrest due to medication causing inability to lie down from vexation: Zhi Mu 1 liang, washed and roasted into powder, make date-meat sized pills. Take one pill with Ginseng decoction. If the physician misdiagnoses this as deficiency vexation and treats wrongly, it may harm fetal qi. (Chan Ru Ji Yan Fang)
9) For long-standing recent phlegmy cough with obstruction below the chest and epigastrium progressing to the viscera: Zhi Mu and Fritillaria Bulb (Chuan Bei Mu) each 1 liang in powder. Croton Seed (Ba Dou) 30 pieces, de-oiled and ground evenly. Each dose a zi size, take with three slices of ginger, dip both sides in medicine, chew and swallow thin, then sleep; a purge will occur early next morning and the cough will immediately stop. Use in strong patients only. One version omits the Croton Seed. (Yi Xue Ji Cheng)
10) Chronic coughing with panting: use Zhi Mu 5 qian (hair removed, sliced, stir-fried between papers), Bitter Apricot Kernel (Ku Xing Ren) 5 qian (soaked in ginger water, peel and tip removed, roasted), decoct together. Separately make pills from equal parts radish seed (Lai Fu Zi) and Bitter Apricot Kernel ground into powder and mixed with rice paste, make pills of 50 each; take with ginger decoction to permanently eliminate the root of the disease.
11) For threatened preterm labor with abdominal pain near term: Zhi Mu 2 liang powdered, make honey pills the size of a paulownia seed. Take 20 pills with congee or water at any time. (Sheng Hui Fang: Zhi Mu Wan)
12) For purpura-like wind disorders: grind Zhi Mu in vinegar and apply topically three times daily. (Wei Sheng Yi Jian Fang)
13) For carbuncles: burn Zhi Mu to preserve its essence, grind to powder and apply to lesions.
14) For cold-damage with floating-slippery pulse, exterior heat with interior cold; or combined disease of the three yang with abdominal fullness, heaviness, difficulty turning, numb mouth, dirty face, delirium, urinary incontinence; sweating increases delirium, inducing collapse when purged, forehead sweats when reduced, cold extremities; spontaneous sweating. Or cold-damage with slippery pulse and collapse with interior heat: Zhi Mu 6 liang, Blue Stone (Shi Qing) 1 jin (crushed), Licorice (Gan Cao) (roasted) 2 liang, polished rice 6 he. Cook the four with 1 dou of water until rice is done, remove dregs and take warm one sheng three times daily. (Shang Han Lun: Bai Hu Tang variant)
15) For cold-damage causing confusion, throat dryness and pain, cracked lips, vomiting of pus and blood: Zhi Mu (roasted) 1 liang, Gypsum Fibrosum (Shi Gao) 2 liang, Scutellaria Root (Huang Qin) (remove dark core), Licorice (Gan Cao) (roasted and rasped) each 3 fen. Coarsely powder and sieve. Each dose 5 qian, water 1 cup and a half, add glutinous rice one spoon, decoct to eight tenths, remove dregs and take warm before meals. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu: Zhi Mu Tang)
16) For cold-damage with stomach heat, vexation, surging rapid pulse, or bloody stools: Zhi Mu 2 qian, Scutellaria Root (Huang Qin) 2 qian, Licorice (Gan Cao) 1 qian. Decoct and take hot. (Bian Que Xin Shu: Zhi Mu Huang Qin Tang)
17) For lung exhaustion with heat where one cannot take tonics: Zhi Mu (stir-fried), Fritillaria Bulb (Chuan Bei Mu) (stir-fried) equal parts, powder and take. (Yi Fang Ji Jie: Er Mu San)
18) For yin-deficiency heat, steaming bones, night sweats, cough, hemoptysis, vexation with easy hunger, pain and heat in knees and feet, red tongue with little coating, and surging rapid pulse: Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai) (stir-fried), Zhi Mu (wine-soaked and stir-fried) each 4 liang, Rehmannia Prepared (Shu Di Huang) (wine-steamed) and Turtle Shell (Gui Ban) (charred with fat) each 6 liang. Powder, make pills with pork spinal marrow and honey about the size of a paulownia seed. Each dose 70 pills on an empty stomach with saline white soup. (Dan Xi Xin Fa: Da Bu Yin Wan)
19) For urinary difficulty without thirst, heat in the lower burner in the blood division: Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai) (bark removed and rasped, washed with wine and dried), Zhi Mu (rasped, wine-washed and dried) each 1 liang, Cinnamon Bark (Rou Gui) 5 fen. Powder finely and form pills with cooked water the size of a paulownia seed. Take 100 pills on an empty stomach with white soup. If urination is slightly smooth but there is stabbing pain in the anterior urethra, some evil substance may be passed as proof. (Lan Shi Mi Cang: Tong Guan Wan)
20) To treat thirst and frequent urination: Zhi Mu 6 fen, Trichosanthes Fruit (Gua Lou) 1 jin, Poria (Fu Ling) 4 fen, Lead Oxide (Qian Dan) 1 fen, Chicken Gizzard Membrane (Ji Nei Jin) 14 pieces. Powder the five and take one small spoonful three times a day. Avoid alcohol, raw lettuce and meat. Later omit the lead oxide and bind with honey; long-term use with barley drink is beneficial but do not stop; avoid sour foods. (Wai Tai)
21) For lily disease after sweating: Lily bulb (Bai He) 7 bulbs (broken), Zhi Mu 3 liang (sliced). First wash the lily and soak overnight until white froth appears, discard the water, then use spring water 2 sheng to boil down to 1 sheng and remove dregs. Separately use spring water 2 sheng to decoct Zhi Mu to 1 sheng and remove dregs. Combine and boil down to 1 sheng 5 he, take warm in divided doses. (Jin Kui Yao Lue: Bai He Zhi Mu Tang)
22) For sudden red film over the eye invading the eye lowering vision: Zhi Mu 3 fen, Cimicifuga? No — actually Sheng Ma (Cimicifuga) 3 fen, Rhubarb (Da Huang) 1/2 liang (rasped and lightly fried), Licorice (Gan Cao) 1/2 liang (roasted slightly red and rasped), Indigo (Da Qing) 3 fen. Coarsely pulverize into powder. Each dose 3 qian, water one medium cup, decoct to six tenths, remove dregs and take warm after meals. (Sheng Hui Fang: Zhi Mu San)
23) Nourishes kidney water, benefits original qi, supplements lower burner deficiency and clears bladder accumulating heat: Zhi Mu 1 liang, Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai) and Coptis (Huang Lian) in equal parts. Powder and form water pills the size of a paulownia seed. Take 50 pills before meals with warm water. (Pu Ji Fang: Kan Li Wan)
24) For warm malaria with a normal pulse and no chills but only fever, bone and joint pain and occasional vomiting: Zhi Mu 6 liang, Licorice (Gan Cao) 2 liang (roasted), Gypsum Fibrosum (Shi Gao) 1 jin, polished rice 2 he, Cinnamon Twig (Gui Zhi) (bark removed) 3 liang. Rasp the herbs, each 5 qian with water half a cup and decoct to eight tenths, remove dregs and take warm until sweating resolves. (Jin Kui Yao Lue: Bai Hu Jia Gui Zhi Tang)
25) For nocturnal emissions and dream-induced seminal discharge: Zhi Mu 1 liang, Phellodendron Bark (Huang Bai) 1 liang (bark removed), Talc (Hua Shi) 3 liang. Powder, make pills with white water and take on an empty stomach with warm wine-salt soup. (Pu Ji Fang: Zhan Meng Dan)

Cultivation and Processing of Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi)
Source
This item is the dried root of the Apiaceae plant Dahurian Angelica (Angelica dahurica (Fisch. ex Hoffm.) Benth. et Hook.f.) or Hangzhou Dahurian Angelica (Angelica dahurica (Fisch. ex Hoffm.) Benth. et Hook.f. var. formosana (Boiss.) Shan et Yuan). It is harvested in summer and autumn when the leaves turn yellow, the fibrous roots and soil are removed, and it is sun-dried or dried at low temperature.
Properties and taste
Pungent, warm.
Appearance
The root is long-conical, 10–25 cm long, 1.5–2.5 cm in diameter. Surface gray-brown or yellow-brown; root head bluntly four-angled or nearly round, with longitudinal wrinkles, lateral root scars and lenticel-like transverse protrusions, some arranged in four longitudinal rows. Apex has a depressed stem scar. Texture firm; fracture surface white or gray-white, mealy; vascular cambium ring brown, nearly square or nearly round; cortex scattered with numerous brown oil-dots. Odor aromatic; taste pungent and slightly bitter.
Effects of Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi)
Functions/Efficacy
This item is the dried root of the Apiaceae plant Dahurian Angelica or Hangzhou Dahurian Angelica.
Mainly treats headache, pain of the supraorbital ridge, toothache, nasal obstruction/sinusitis, cold-damp abdominal pain, intestinal wind and hemorrhoids/anal fistula, red or white vaginal discharge, carbuncles and sores, dry itchy skin, scabies and tinea.
Meridians
Enters
Lung meridian
,
Spleen meridian
,
Stomach meridian
.
Indications
Expels wind, dries dampness, reduces swelling, and relieves pain. Treats headache, supraorbital ridge pain, toothache, nasal obstruction/sinusitis, cold-damp abdominal pain, intestinal wind and hemorrhoids/anal fistula, red or white vaginal discharge, carbuncles and sores, dry itchy skin, scabies and tinea.
① 'Ben Jing': Treats women's abnormal red and white vaginal discharge, blood obstruction causing swelling of the genitals, alternating cold and heat, wind of the head invading the eyes causing tears, promotes flesh growth and moisturizes the skin.
② 'Bie Lu': Cures prolonged thirst due to wind-evil (or possibly prolonged diarrhea), vomiting, fullness of the two flanks, wind pain with dizziness of the head, and itchy eyes.
③ 'Yao Xing Lun': Treats stabbing pain in the heart and abdomen and abdominal blood stasis pain, dispels wind-evil, is indicated for women's metrorrhagia and retching, clears the eyes and stops tearing, treats women's prolonged spotting and low back and abdominal pain; able to corrode pus.
④ 'Ri Hua Zi Ben Cao': Treats red eyes and ocular pterygium, secures threatened abortion and prevents slippage, breaks old blood and replenishes new blood, treats mastitis, back swellings, scrofula, intestinal wind, hemorrhoids and fistula, promotes pus discharge, treats ulcers, scabies and tinea, relieves pain and generates flesh, removes facial pockmarks and scars.
⑤ 'Dian Nan Ben Cao': Expels wandering wind of the skin, stops stomach cold and abdominal pain from cold, and relieves whole-body cold-damp pain.
⑥ 'Compendium of Materia Medica (Bencao Gangmu)': Treats nasal obstruction, epistaxis, toothache, supraorbital pain, large-intestine wind constipation, bloody urine, women's blood-wind dizziness and irregular menses, reversal of the stomach with vomiting; antidote for arsenic poisoning, snakebite, and knife or arrow wounds.
Dosage and Administration
Internal: decoct, 3–10 g; or used in pills or powders.
External: appropriate amount, grind to powder and sprinkle or mix into a poultice.
Precautions and Contraindications
Contraindicated for those with yin deficiency and blood-heat.
① 'Bencao Jing Jizhu': Angelica sinensis (Dang Gui) acts as its assistant; incompatible with Xuan Fu Hua (Inula Flower).
② 'Bencao Jing Shu': Contraindicated when vomiting is due to excess fire. Do not use for red or white vaginal discharge caused by yin deficiency with blazing fire and blood heat. When an abscess has ulcerated, gradually reduce and stop.
Formulas using Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi)
① To treat headache and eye pain: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) 4 qian, raw Aconite (Chuan Wu) 1 qian. Grind into powder; each dose about one small pellet ('zi'), taken with tea. For some with eye pain, first hold water in the mouth, then insufflate this into the nose for faster effect. (From Zhu's Collected Tested Prescriptions: Baizhi Powder)
② To treat various wind-induced vertigo, women before and after childbirth suddenly attacked by wind-evil, heaviness of head and eyes and blood-wind headache, sudden cold-warm changes, clouded spirit, and cold-damage wind-dizziness: Fragrant Bai Zhi (Xiang Bai Zhi) (soak and wash with boiling water four to five times) made into powder, bind with refined honey into pills the size of a bead. Take one pill per dose, often chewed with Schizonepeta (Jing Jie) and waxed tea. (From Bai Yi Xuan Fang: Du Liang Wan)
③ To treat hemicranial headache: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi), Asarum (Xi Xin), Gypsum (Shi Gao), Frankincense (Ru Xiang), Myrrh (Mo Yao) (oil removed). These ingredients in equal parts, made into a fine powder, insufflate into the nose; if left-sided pain, insufflate into the right nostril; if right-sided pain, insufflate into the left. (From Zhong Fu Tang Selected Good Prescriptions: Baizhi-Xixin Nasal Powder)
④ To treat supraorbital rim pain due to wind-heat with phlegm: Baical Skullcap (Huang Qin) (fried with wine) and Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi). Make into powder; take 2 qian with clear tea. (From Danxi Xinfa)
⑤ To treat nasal obstruction/sinusitis: Magnolia Flower (Xin Yi), Saposhnikovia (Fang Feng), Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) each 8 fen, Cocklebur Fruit (Cang Er Zi) 1 qian 2 fen, Szechuan Lovage Root (Chuan Xiong) 5 fen, Northern Asarum (Xi Xin) 7 fen, Licorice (Gan Cao) 3 fen. Decoction in water, take four doses in succession. Avoid beef. (From Yang Yi Da Quan)
⑥ To treat intestinal wind: Fragrant Bai Zhi (Xiang Bai Zhi) finely powdered, mixed with rice gruel and taken. (From Bai Yi Xuan Fang)
⑦ To treat constipation due to intestinal wind: Fragrant Bai Zhi (Xiang Bai Zhi) fried and powdered, 2 qian per dose, take with rice soup with a little honey, take two consecutive doses. (From Shi Bian Liang Fang)
⑧ To treat hemorrhoidal swelling and pain: first smoke with Gleditsia Fruit (Zhu Ya Zao), then mix Dahurian Angelica Root powder with goose bile and apply. (From Yi Fang Zhai Yao)
⑨ To treat leukorrhea, intestinal putrid pus, persistent urinary dribbling with severe foul smell, and cold abdominal pain requiring pus drainage: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) 1 liang, Single-leaf Red Mallow Root 2 liang, White Peony Root (Bai Shao) (white variety), Alum (Bai Fan) each 0.5 liang (alum calcined until dry, then separately ground). Make into powder and roll into wax-coated pills the size of a catalpa seed; take on an empty stomach or before meals with rice gruel, ten to fifteen pills until the pus is exhausted, then use other medicines to tonify. (From Ben Cao Yan Yi)
⑩ To treat swelling-from-toxin heat and pain: mix Bai Zhi powder with vinegar and apply as a poultice. (From Wei Sheng Yi Jian Fang)
⑾ To treat carbuncles and red swelling: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) and Rhubarb (Da Huang) in equal parts. Make into powder; take 2 qian with rice gruel. (From Jing Yan Fang)
⑿ To treat knife and arrow wounds: chew Fragrant Bai Zhi (Xiang Bai Zhi) to a pulp and apply. (From Bin Hu Ji Jian Fang)
⒀ To treat headache: Gypsum (Shi Gao) and Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) each 2 qian, Mint Leaves (Bo He) and Mirabilite (Mang Xiao) each 3 qian, Turmeric (Yu Jin) 1 qian. Make into an extremely fine powder, hold water in the mouth, and retain it in the nose. (From Lan Shi Mi Cang: Baizhi Powder)
⒁ To treat unilateral headache: Gleditsia Fruit (Zhu Ya Zao) (remove fibrous membrane), Fragrant Bai Zhi (Xiang Bai Zhi), White Aconite (Bai Fu Zi) in equal parts. Make into powder. Each dose 1 qian, taken with waxed tea after meals. (From Xu Ben Shi Fang)
⒂ To treat unbearable headache, whether unilateral or bilateral, and to treat red eye and toothache: Dried Ginger (Gan Jiang) and Fragrant Bai Zhi each half liang, Artemisia Fruit (Hao Jiao Zi) 1 qian. Make into a fine powder. Use about 0.5 qian daily divided into three doses, insufflate finely into the nose and massage both temples; the pain stops immediately. (From Ji Feng Pu Ji Fang: Tong Ding San)
⒃ To treat severe eye pain: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi), Red Peony Root (Chi Shao), Saposhnikovia (Fang Feng), Asarum (Xi Xin) in equal parts. Make into powder. Each dose 1 qian with one cup of water and 2 qian rock sugar; remove dregs and take warm at any time. (From Xu Ben Shi Fang)
⒄ To treat persistent clear nasal discharge: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) finely powdered, mixed with mashed scallion white into pills the size of a small bean. Take 20 pills per dose with tea. (From Zheng Zhi Zhun Sheng: Baizhi Pills)
⒅ To treat gastric pain from ulcers: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi), White Peony Root (Bai Shao), Bletilla (Bai Ji) each 10–30 g, White Cardamom (Bai Dou Kou) 6–12 g. One dose daily, decoct in water and divide for administration. (From Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine 1983(12):34 — Si Bai Decoction)
⒆ To treat continuous metrorrhagia: Fragrant Bai Zhi (Xiang Bai Zhi) 1.5 liang, Dragon Bone (Long Gu) 1 liang, Schizonepeta Leaves (Jing Jie Ye) 0.5 liang. Grind into a fine powder. Each dose 2 qian, taken with warm wine; may also be taken with rice gruel or soup before meals. (From Yang Family Recipes: Fang Xiang San)
⒇ To treat chronic knee rheumatism ("crane knee wind"): take fresh Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi), decoct in wine to a paste, store in a ceramic jar. Daily take 2 qian of the paste with aged wine; additionally apply 2–3 qian topically to the affected area until it subsides. (From Waike Quansheng Ji)
(21) To treat infantile mastitis and nipple erosion extending to surrounding tissue: Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) 2 qian, Oyster Shell Powder (Mu Li) 5 qian, Borneol (Bing Pian) 2 fen. Make into fine powder and apply to the affected area. (From Wai Ke Zhen Quan: Baizhi Powder)
(22) To treat poisonous snakebite: Fragrant Bai Zhi (Xiang Bai Zhi) powdered. Mix with Ophiopogon decoction (Mai Dong) to drink; in urgent cases freshly drawn water is acceptable. (From Hong's Collected Tested Prescriptions)
(23) To treat metal or iron injuries and tetanus: Coptis (Huang Lian), Areca Nut (Bing Lang), Aucklandia (Mu Xiang), and Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) in equal parts. Make into a fine powder and apply to the wounded area; bleeding will stop. For women's postpartum bleeding, mix 1 qian with a boy's urine; for visceral toxic bleeding, decoct in water and take. (From Ji Feng Pu Ji Fang: Baizhi Powder)
(24) To treat fish-bone lodging: Pinellia (Ban Xia) 5 liang (washed), Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) 5 liang. Pound and sieve these two items. Take one spoonful (approximate measure); it will induce vomiting and expel the bone. Avoid mutton and maltose. (From Wai Tai)
Dietary Therapy Recipes
1. Stewed Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) with Bird's Nest
Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) 9 g, bird's nest 9 g, rock sugar to taste. Double-boil Bai Zhi and bird's nest until very soft, strain off dregs. Add rock sugar to taste and double-boil briefly; take 1–2 times daily. Functions: tonifies the lung and nourishes yin, stops cough and stops bleeding.
2. Mint, Cocklebur and Dahurian Angelica Tea
Mint (Bo He) 6 g, Cocklebur Fruit (Cang Er Zi) 12 g, Magnolia Flower (Xin Yi) 6 g, Dahurian Angelica Root (Bai Zhi) 6 g, Scallion white (Cong Bai) 3 stalks, Tea leaf 2 g. Put all the above herbs into a pot, decoct, strain and use the liquid. Drink as a tea substitute.
Efficacy: disperses wind and opens the orifices. Indications: treats rhinitis, sinusitis and related disorders.

Cultivation and processing of Asarum (Xi Xin)
Source
The whole herb with roots of Aristolochiaceae plants Liao Asarum (Liao Xi Xin), Asarum (Xi Xin) and Hansung Asarum (Han Cheng Xi Xin).
When transplanted it is harvested after 3–5 years of field growth; when direct-seeded in the field it is harvested after 5–6 years. In mid-September dig up the entire root system, remove the soil, tie into bunches of 1–2 kg each, place in a cool shaded place to air-dry, then pack into storage.
Property and flavor
Acrid; warm; slightly toxic
Processing
Remove impurities, spray with water to moisten, promptly cut into sections, and air-dry.
Lei Gong Pao Zhi Lun: When using Xi Xin, pick off paired leaves one by one, for they harm people when taken. Must remove head soil; soak in gourd water overnight, in the morning strain it out, sun-dry and use.
Appearance
(1) Liao Asarum (Liao Xi Xin)
Usually curled into a mass. Rhizome irregularly cylindrical, 1–10 cm long, 2–4 mm in diameter; surface gray-brown, rough, with nodes, internodes 2–3 mm long. Roots fine, densely produced on the nodes, 10–20 cm long, about 1 mm in diameter; surface gray-yellow; brittle, breaks easily, fracture yellow-white. Basal leaf petiole long, smooth, intact; when leaves are spread flat they are ovate-cordate or reniform-cordate, apex acute or obtuse, base deeply cordate, 4–9 cm long, 5–13 cm wide; upper surface deep green with hairs along the veins, underside densely hairy. Flowers occasionally seen, purple-brown, hemispherical; perianth lobes reflexed from the base and appressed to the perianth tube. Fragrant aroma, pungent taste, slightly numbs the tongue.
(2) Asarum (Xi Xin)
Similar to Liao Asarum but the rhizome is more slender, 5–15 cm long, 1–3 mm in diameter, internodes 0.2–1 cm long; leaf blades thinner, cordate. Odor weaker.
(3) Hansung Asarum (Han Cheng Xi Xin)
Very similar to Asarum, but usually with denser hairs on the underside of the leaf and hairs on the petiole. In cultivated varieties the hair density varies greatly, making it hard to distinguish from Asarum.
Therapeutic effects of Asarum (Xi Xin)
Functions
The whole herb with roots of Aristolochiaceae plants Liao Asarum (Liao Xi Xin), Asarum (Xi Xin) and Hansung Asarum (Han Cheng Xi Xin).
Mainly treats wind-cold headache, nasal obstruction/sinusitis, toothache, phlegm-fluid cough with counterflow, and wind-damp painful obstruction.
Meridians
Lung meridian; Kidney meridian; Heart meridian; Liver meridian; Gallbladder meridian; Spleen meridian.
Indications
Dispel wind, disperse cold, promote urination/resolve fluid retention, open orifices. Treats wind-cold headache, nasal congestion/sinusitis, toothache, phlegm-fluid cough with counterflow, and wind-damp painful obstruction.
(1) Disperse wind-cold: used for wind-cold common cold or headaches due to wind-cold; can be paired with Ephedra (Ma Huang) or Ledebouriella root (Gao Ben).
(2) Warm the channels and relieve pain: used for muscle and joint pain due to cold invading the collaterals.
(3) Warm and transform cold phlegm: used for chronic bronchitis with abundant thin phlegm.
(4) Open the lung orifices: used for rhinitis and sinusitis.
Dosage and administration
Internal use: decocted, 1.5–9 g; ground to powder, 1–3 g.
External use: appropriate amount, powdered and blown into the nose, packed into the ear, applied to the navel; or decocted water used for gargling.
Precautions and contraindications
Contraindicated in qi deficiency with spontaneous sweating, headache due to blood deficiency, cough due to yin deficiency, etc.
① Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu: Zeng Qing and zaogen are adjuvants. Contraindicated with wolf’s bane, Cornus officinalis, Astragalus membranaceus. Avoid talc and xiaoshi. Opposes Aconitum.
② Yao Xing Lun: avoid raw lettuce.
③ Ben Cao Jing Shu: In general, for diseases of internal heat and fire rising upwards, excessive heat above and deficiency below, qi deficiency with sweating, headache due to blood deficiency, cough due to yin deficiency, this herb is prohibited.
④ De Pei Ben Cao: contraindicated in wind-heat or yin deficiency.
Formulas containing Asarum (Xi Xin)
① For wind-cold headache, with pain like bursting, pulse faint, wiry and tight:
Asarum (Xi Xin) 1 liang (clean),
Ligusticum chuanxiong (Chuan Xiong) 1 liang,
Prepared aconite (Fu Zi) (processed) ½ liang (clean),
Ephedra (Ma Huang) 1 fen. Cut finely, include roots, add scallion white (Cong Bai), fresh ginger (Sheng Jiang), jujube (Da Zao). Each dose 5 qian, 1.5 bowls of water, decoct to 1 bowl, take in three doses consecutively. (Pu Ji Fang, Xi Xin San)
② For migraine:
Realgar (Xiong Huang) (ground),
Asarum (Xi Xin) (remove shoots and leaves, make into powder) equal parts. Grind the two together evenly. Each dose a character-sized amount; if left side pain, blow into right nostril; if right side pain, blow into left nostril. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu, Zhi Ling San)
③ For common cold with nasal congestion:
Asarum (Xi Xin),
Perilla leaf (Zi Su Ye),
Saposhnikovia root (Fang Feng),
Bitter apricot kernel (Ku Xing Ren),
Platycodon root (Jie Geng),
Mint (Bo He),
Mulberry root bark (Sang Bai Pi). Decoction. (Fang Mai Zheng Zong)
④ For externally contracted cold not resolved, water accumulation under the heart, dry heaves, fever with cough, or thirst, diarrhea, dysphagia, or difficult urination; lower abdominal distention, or shortness of breath:
Ephedra (Ma Huang) (nodes removed),
White peony root (Bai Shao Yao),
Asarum (Xi Xin),
Dried ginger (Gan Jiang),
Licorice (Gan Cao) (honey-fried),
Cinnamon twig (Gui Zhi) (peel removed) each 3 liang,
Schisandra (Wu Wei Zi) half sheng,
Pinellia (Ban Xia) half sheng (washed). Take the eight ingredients with one dou of water, first boil Ephedra, reduce by 2 sheng, skim the foam, add the remaining herbs, boil down to 3 sheng, strain. Warmly take one sheng. (Shang Han Lun, Xiao Qing Long Tang)
⑤ For nasal obstruction: a small amount of powdered Asarum (Xi Xin) blown into the nose. (Pu Ji Fang)
⑥ For chronic toothache not healing:
Asarum (Xi Xin) (remove leaves and shoots),
Long pepper (Bi Ba). Equal parts, coarsely pounded and sifted. Each use half qian, one bowl of water, decoct until several boils, gargle hot and spit cold. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu, Xi Xin Tang)
⑦ For toothache:
Schizonepeta (Jing Jie),
Asarum (Xi Xin),
Beehive (Luofengfang) equal parts. Coarsely powdered, use three qian per dose, one large bowl of water, decoct to 70%, strain and warm gargle and spit cold. (Yu Yao Yuan Fang, Xi Xin San)
⑧ For toothache:
Asarum (Xi Xin) 1 qian,
Phellodendron bark (Huang Bai) 1 qian. Decoction used to rinse the mouth; do not swallow. (Jilin Zhong Cao Yao)
⑨ For phlegm-fluid where qi is driven downwards but causes coughing and chest fullness:
Poria (Fu Ling) 4 liang,
Licorice (Gan Cao),
Dried ginger (Gan Jiang),
Asarum (Xi Xin) each 3 liang,
Schisandra (Wu Wei Zi) half sheng. Take the five ingredients with eight sheng of water, boil down to 3 sheng, strain. Warmly take half a sheng three times daily. (Jin Kui Yao Lue, Ling Gan Wu Wei Jiang Xin Tang)
⑩ For Shao Yin disease, early stage with subsequent fever and a submerged pulse:
Ephedra (Ma Huang) 2 liang (nodes removed),
Asarum (Xi Xin) 2 liang,
Prepared aconite (Fu Zi) one piece (processed, peel removed, broken into eight slices). Take the three herbs with one dou of water, boil Ephedra first, reduce by 2 sheng, skim foam, add the others, boil down to 3 sheng, strain. Warmly take one sheng, three times daily. (Shang Han Lun, Ma Huang Fu Zi Xi Xin Tang)
⑾ For wind entering the abdomen with cutting pain and vexation:
Asarum (Xi Xin),
Evodia fruit (Wu Zhu Yu),
Dried ginger (Gan Jiang) each ½ liang,
Dong quai (Dang Gui),
Saposhnikovia root (Fang Feng) each 1 liang,
Peony root (Shao Yao) 2 liang. Grind into powder; use half liang per dose with 2 liang water, boil to 1 liang, warm and divide into three doses, take in succession. (Yuan He Ji Yong Jing, Xi Xin Tang)
⑿ For children’s mouth ulcers: powdered Asarum (Xi Xin) mixed with vinegar, applied to the navel. (Wei Sheng Jia Bao Fang)
⒀ For halitosis and hidden dental abscess pain: decoct Asarum (Xi Xin) to a strong juice, hold hot and spit cold. (Sheng Hui Fang)
⒁ For deafness: powdered Asarum (Xi Xin) mixed with yellow wax into pills the size of mouse droppings. Wrap one pill in cotton and insert; avoid anger. (Gong Shi Ying Yuan Fang, Cong Er Wan)
⒂ For deficient cold causing hiccup and poor appetite:
Asarum (Xi Xin) (remove leaves) ½ liang,
Clove (Ding Xiang) 2.5 qian. Make into powder. Each dose 1 qian, take with persimmon calyx decoction. (Ben Cao Gang Mu)
⒃ For sudden fainting and loss of consciousness: powdered Asarum (Xi Xin) blown into the nose. (Shi Yi De Xiao Fang)
⒄ For pediatric acute fright and refusal (symptoms: facial pallor, startle pain, inability to speak; or neck rigidity with danger signs; or sudden crying at night): use equal parts Asarum (Xi Xin) and cinnamon heart (Gui Xin), powdered; give a small amount in the child’s mouth.
⒅ For oral sores: equal parts Asarum (Xi Xin) and Coptis (Huang Lian) powdered. First clean the lesion with a cloth, apply the powder; when saliva is expelled it is cured. (Wei Sheng Yi Jian Fang)
⒆ For nasal polyps: periodically blow powdered Asarum (Xi Xin) into the nose.
⒇ Formula for sudden cold-induced cough:
Asarum (Xi Xin) ½ liang (pounded to powder),
Bitter apricot kernel (Ku Xing Ren) ½ liang (soaked in water, remove skin and tips and double kernels, stir-fry with bran until slightly yellow, grind to a paste). Melt ½ liang wax in a pan, then add 1 fen ghee, add Asarum and apricot kernel, roll into pills the size of a date. At any time, wrap one pill in cotton and hold in the mouth to dissolve and swallow the saliva. (Sheng Hui Fang)
(21) For sudden violent wind-stroke with fainting, locked jaw, inability to swallow medicine:
Asarum (Xi Xin) (wash off soil and leaves),
Zhu Ya Zao (Zhu Ya Zao) (remove seed) each 1 qian. Grind to fine powder; dab a little on a twisted paper and insert into the nose, wait for sneeze, then administer medicine. (Ji Sheng Xu Fang)
(22) For nasal obstruction and loss of smell: Asarum (Xi Xin) (remove shoots and leaves),
Melon peduncle (Gua Di) each 1 fen. Pound and sift into a powder and blow a small amount into the nose.
(23) For dental ulcerations:
Asarum (Xi Xin) (remove shoots and leaves),
Toad venom (Chan Su) (stir-fried dry),
Melon peduncle (Gua Di),
Coptis (Huang Lian) (remove roots) each 1 fen. Pound and sift into powder. Each use 1 qian spoonful, apply to the tooth, three to five times daily. (Formulas 8–10 from Sheng Ji Zong Lu)
(24) For toothache:
Asarum (Xi Xin) and saltpetre (Pen Xiao) each 1 qian,
Realgar (Xiong Huang) 5 fen,
Zhu Ya Zao two pieces. Make into powder, mix with one clove of garlic and roll into pills the size of a catalpa seed. Use one pill, wrap in cotton; if left tooth pains, plug left ear; if right, plug right ear. (Wai Ke Da Cheng)
(25) For trachoma (queremia), adults or children, chronic:
Asarum (Xi Xin),
Kochia fruit (Di Fu Zi),
Cassia seed (Jue Ming Zi),
Pine resin (Song Zhi) each 2 liang. Pound and sift into powder. After meals, take one qian with bamboo-leaf decoction.
(26) For sudden deafness: Asarum (Xi Xin) 1 fen,
Cattail pollen (Pu Huang) 1 fen,
Bitter apricot kernel (Ku Xing Ren) 3 fen (soaked, skins and tips removed, kernels prepared), fermented malt powder (Qu Mo) 3 fen (lightly fried). Pound and sift into powder, grind apricot kernel into a paste, combine and roll into a pill the size of a date, wrap in cotton and insert into the ear, change once daily until cured. (Formulas 25–26 from Sheng Hui Fang)
(27) For ear congestion, ear pain, discharge of pus and blood from the ear:
Asarum (Xi Xin) (remove shoots, file),
Prepared aconite (Fu Zi) (processed, split, remove navel and peel) each 1 fen. Pound and sift into powder, mix with one qian spoonful of scallion juice, wrap in cotton and insert into the ear. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu)
(28) For leukoderma: wash with warm water from a tree hollow, then pound Asarum (Xi Xin) and oyster shell (Mu Li) equal parts into powder, mix with lard and apply to the leukoderma, three times daily at night. (Sheng Hui Fang)
(29) For snakebite: Asarum (Xi Xin),
Angelica dahurica (Bai Zhi) each 5 qian,
Realgar (Xiong Huang) 2.5 qian. Make into powder, add a little musk (She Xiang). Each dose 2 qian, take with warm wine. (Wei Sheng Yi Jian Fang)
(30) For elderly people who easily feel drowsy in spring:
Asarum (Xi Xin) 2 liang (remove soil),
Ligusticum chuanxiong (Chuan Xiong) 2 liang,
Ku Cao (bitter herb) ½ liang (stir-fried). Grind into powder; each dose one large qian with one bowl of water, decoct to 60%, sip hot. Can be taken regularly. (Yang Lao Feng Qin Shu)

Autumn Stone (Qiu Shi)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E7%A7%8B%E7%9F%B3
Name
Depositum Urinae Praeparatum, Urine Deposit Preparation
Qiudan Stone (Qiūdānshí), Qiubing (Qiūbīng), Pale Qiushi (Dàn Qiūshí), Qiushi Dan (Qiūshí Dān)
Qiubing (Qiūbīng)
Qiushidan (Qiūshí Dān)
Qiudan Stone (Qiūdānshí)
Pale Qiushi (Dàn Qiūshí)
Cultivation and Preparation of Qiushi (Qiūshí)
Source
Is
Renzhongbai (Rénzhōngbái)
and
salt (Shíyán)
as a processed product. In ancient times it was also made by processing
human urine (Rénniào)
,
autumn-dew water (Qiūlùshuǐ)
and
gypsum (Shígāo)
and others.
Habitat and Distribution
Mainly produced in East China.
Nature and Taste
Salty, cold.
Processing
There are two types: Pale Qiushi (Dàn Qiūshí) and Saline Qiushi (Xián Qiūshí).
Pale Qiushi (Dàn Qiūshí): take washed and sun-dried renzhongbai (Rénzhōngbái), grind into powder, add Bletilla (Bái Jí) and starch water as auxiliary materials, mix, then press with a mold into small square blocks and sun-dry.
Saline Qiushi (Xián Qiūshí): take salt (Shíyán) and clean spring water, boil and filter, heat the filtrate to evaporate and dry into a powdery frost called Qiushi frost. Then place the Qiushi frost in a lidded porcelain bowl, calcine over a stove for two hours, cool and it will congeal into a solid block.
1. Ye Mengde (Ye Mengde), Shuiyun Lu (Shuǐ Yún Lù): Those who refine Qiushi in the world rely only on fire refinement; this medicine must undergo both yin and yang refinements to be supreme. Yang refinement method: use more than ten shi of human urine, each placed in wooden barrels; for each shi add one bowl of soap-pod (Zàojiá) juice, stir rapidly with a bamboo pole hundreds or thousands of times, wait for clarification, discard the clear liquid and keep the sediment, and make another barrel and stir until clear as before; take one or two dou of the concentrated juice, filter clean, put into a pot and simmer until dry, scrape off and pound finely, then dissolve with clear broth and boil, pour over a paper-lined winnowing tray and boil again, repeat several times until the color is white as snow, then use a sand box to consolidate and calcine with fire into substance, pour out; if the medicine is not yet formed, calcine one or two more times until the color is like translucent jade, grind finely, put into the sand box to compress, apply top heat and nurture for seven days and nights, take out and spread on earth to remove fire-toxins and make powder. Yin refinement method: use four or five shi of human urine in a large jar, add half new water, stir many times, let settle, discard the clear liquid and keep the sediment, add new water and stir and clarify again until there is no foul smell and the settled material is like greasy powder, then sun-dry, scrape off and grind again, mix with a boy's breast milk into a paste, sun-dry fiercely, repeat this nine times to make the powder.
2. Bencao Mengquan (Běncǎo Méngquán): In autumn collect children's urine; for each barrel of urine add seven qian of gypsum powder, stir twice with mulberry branches, after about half ke the essence gradually sinks to the bottom and the clear liquid with white floats on top; wait for clarification and pour off the liquid, then add fresh urine and mix as before, add powder and stir, pour off leaving the sediment—do not deviate. After all urine has been processed and the clear liquid poured off, then add one barrel of autumn-dew water and stir with a mulberry branch, let stand and pour off again; repeat several times to wash away dregs and impurities and remove the salty foul taste. When finished, seal heavily with paper and wait until dry and firmly congealed, then take out whole. The light, clear essence will float and congeal on the surface and be white in quality. The original gypsum powder and other heavy turbid dregs will sink and gather at the bottom, being blackish and dull; keep the surface portion and scrape off and discard the bottom. If instead one seals in a jar and gently heats for half a ke, although the color becomes very white the nature becomes warm and it is ultimately inferior to sun-dried material.
3. Benjing Fengyuan (Běnjīng Fèngyuán): Yin collection method for Qiushi: form dozens of lead balls the size of a lead pellet, each made of two pieces pressed together with many drilled holes, place them into the urine barrels to soak, each day pour off the overnight urine and replace with fresh urine to continue soaking; at the autumn harvest collect them and store in a lead container. Yang refining of Qiushi: take hundreds of pairs of straw sandals, the older the better, wash and sun-bleach in running water for seven days to remove yellowing, then soak them in urine barrels, sun-expose by day and soak by night for about a month, dry in the sun, burn to ash in strong sun and stir frequently to burn thoroughly, pour boiling water to leach and clarify for several days, dry the pot, add rainwater to dissolve and cook, filter through layers of bamboo sieves and paper to clarify and repeat for over half a month, then boil dry in a silver can until the color is white as frost; collect into lead containers. Another yang refinement method: use a boy's urine, boil in a pot until dry; the pot should first be heated red-hot and greased with fragrant oil and washed so the residue will not stick and damage the pot, initially like oil residue, place into a yang-cheng can or small iron cauldron, calcine to red, dissolve with hot water and place into a spouted pot, cover the spout with straw and slowly pour out, underlay with a bamboo sieve lined with paper to filter clear, then dry over gentle fire and collect into lead containers, after which it will not dissolve.
Characteristics
A powdery aggregate. Appears as small square blocks or flattened round shapes, some often stamped with red characters indicating Pale Qiushi, diameter 1.5–2.2 cm. White or gray-white, surface flat but not smooth; dull, opaque. Hard and brittle, easily crushed, fracture powdery and uneven. Slight odor, mild taste. Insoluble in water. The best specimens are intact blocks, dry and without salty or foul odor. Pale Qiushi (as described in Benjing Fengyuan) is often gray-white or light-red small square blocks with a not-very-smooth, dull surface; hard and brittle; mild taste. The best are intact, dry and without salty or foul odor.
Effects of Qiushi (Qiūshí)
Functions
Is a processed product of renzhongbai (Rénzhōngbái) and salt (Shíyán).
Main indications: bone-steaming consumptive fever, cough, coughing blood, swollen and painful throat, dysphagia with regurgitation, seminal emission, leukorrhea, turbid urine with dripping, and female red or white leukorrhea.
Channels
Enters the Lung meridian and Kidney meridian.
Indications
Nourishes yin and reduces fire. Treats bone-steaming consumptive fever, cough, coughing blood, swollen and painful throat, dysphagia with regurgitation, seminal emission, leukorrhea, turbid dripping urination, and female red or white leukorrhea.
1. Bencao Mengquan (Běncǎo Méngquán): nourishes kidney water, nourishes the dantian (dān tián), calms and harmonizes the five viscera, moistens the triple burner, reduces cough with thick reverse phlegm, dispels the pathogenic heat of bone-steaming, softens accumulations and hard masses, brightens the eyes and clarifies the heart.
2. Yixue Rumun (Yīxué Rùmén, Medical Introduction): treats emaciation with chronic cough, dimmed vision and dizziness, abdominal distension and fullness with panting, soreness of the loins and knees, seminal emission and leukorrhea.
3. Gangmu (Gāngmù, Compendium): treats deficiency consumptive cold disorders, frequent and involuntary urination.
4. Bencao Beiyao (Běncǎo Bèiyào): nourishes yin and reduces fire.
5. Benjing Fengyuan (Běnjīng Fèngyuán): can nourish yin and reduce fire without harming the stomach, tonify the original fire of the lower source, disperse blood stasis, assist yin essence, suppress pathogenic fire and return true yang, stop deficiency-heat cough with blood, and treat bone-steaming consumptive disease.
6. Modern Practical Chinese Medicine: for internal use mostly employ Pale Qiushi (Dàn Qiūshí) for chronic oral and laryngeal inflammations; Saline Qiushi (Xián Qiūshí) is more often used externally for oral and pharyngeal ulcers.
Usage and Dosage
Internal use: in pills or powders, 4.5–9 g.
External use: grind to powder and sprinkle.
Cautions
Contraindicated in those with spleen and stomach deficiency-cold.
Qiushi (Qiūshí) Formulas
1. For male and female deficiency and emaciation: Qiushi (Qiūshí) 1 liang, dried Shanyao (Shānyào) 1 liang. Grind to powder; separately mix Shanyao with wine into a paste, form pills the size of a wutong seed and coat with dried Shanyao. Take twenty pills with warm wine or rice gruel as desired. (Hong’s Collected Tested Formulas)
2. To tonify kidney water and treat deficiency: True Qiushi (Zhēn Qiūshí) 10 liang, white Poria (Bái Fúlíng) 4 liang, lotus seed (Liánzǐ) 4 liang, Shanyao (Shānyào) 4 liang, fennel seed (Xiǎo Huí Xiāng) 2 liang. Make into wine pills and take with plain rice decoction on an empty stomach. For women add raw Rehmannia (Shēng Dìhuáng) 2 liang, prepared Rehmannia (Shú Dìhuáng) 4 liang, Chuanxiong (Chuānxiōng) 3 liang, and use jujube (Dàzǎo) flesh to form the pills. (He’s Jisheng Lun, Qiushi Dan)
3. For excessive thinking or sexual indulgence damaging heart qi, causing seminal emission and frequent urination: Qiushi (Qiūshí) and white Poria (Bái Fúlíng) each 4 liang, lotus seed (Liánzǐ) and gorgon seed (Qiànshí) each 2 liang. Powder, steam with jujube flesh and form pills the size of a wutong seed. Take thirty pills with saline broth on an empty stomach. (Yonglei Qianfang, Qiushi Four-Essence Pills)
4. For leukorrhea and seminal emission: Qiushi (Qiūshí) 1 liang, white Poria (Bái Fúlíng) 5 qian, Cuscuta (Tǔsīzǐ, fried) 5 qian. Powder, use one cup of boiling decoction and one cup of well water to cook to a paste and form pills the size of a wutong seed. Take one hundred pills with saline broth. (Zheng Family Heirloom Formula, Qiushi Jiaogan Dan)
5. For turbid qi separating clear, essence scattering and forming dripping turbid urine with yellow, white or dark red like fat or honey oil: Qiushi (Qiūshí), deer antler glue (Lùjiǎojiāo, fried), mantis egg case (Sāng Piāoxiāo, roasted) each half liang, white Poria (Bái Fúlíng) 1 liang. Powder, make into paste and form pills the size of a wutong seed. Take fifty pills with ginseng (Rénshēn) soup. (Renzhai Zhizhi Fang, Qiushi Pills)
6. For red or white leukorrhea: true Qiushi (Zhēn Qiūshí) ground to powder, steam and mash jujube (Dàzǎo) flesh and form pills the size of a wutong seed. Take sixty pills with vinegar decoction on an empty stomach. (Zhaiyuan Fang)
7. For dysphagia with regurgitation: Qiushi (Qiūshí), each dose one qian, take with plain broth. (Yifang Zhaiyao)

Bai Du Cao (Bai Du Cao)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E8%B4%A5%E6%AF%92%E8%8D%89
Ear-leaved Golden-hair Bracken (Er ye jin mao luo jue)
Cultivation and processing of Baiducao (Bai Du Cao)
Source
From the rhizome or whole herb of Ear-leaved Golden-hair Bracken (Er ye jin mao luo jue), a plant of the family Dennstaedtiaceae. Collected year-round or in summer and autumn, washed clean, used fresh or sun-dried.
[Morphology]
Plants 8–22 cm high. Rhizome creeping, together with the bases of the petioles densely covered with rust-red, linear-lanceolate scales and white soft hairs. Leaves nearly clustered; petiole wiry, rigid, 5–10 cm long, chestnut-colored, densely covered from the base upward with long pale-brown soft hairs; leaf blades thick-papery, lanceolate, 5–15 cm long, 1.5–4 cm wide, the apical pinna largest, up to 3 cm long, once-pinnate; pinnae 3–11 pairs, alternate, ovate or oblong-ovate, base cordate, asymmetric, sometimes with small auriculate protrusions, apex obtuse, base with short stalks, margins entire, adaxial surface dark green sparsely covered with soft hairs, abaxial surface densely covered with rust-colored soft hairs. Sori linear, borne along both sides of the lateral veins, hidden among the soft hairs; indusia absent.
[Habitat and distribution]
Ecology: grows on dry rocks on mountain slopes at elevations of 900–2000 m.
Distribution: occurs in Northeast China, North China, Northwest China, Southwest China and in provinces such as Shandong, Henan, Hubei.
Nature and taste
Bitter; cold
Characteristics
Rhizome densely covered with rust-yellow narrow lanceolate long scales. Petioles chestnut-brown, covered with soft hairs up to the rachis. Leaf blades thick-papery, 5–15 cm long, 1.5–4 cm wide, once-pinnate with an odd number of pinnae, pinnae bases deeply cordate, sometimes with 1–2 small auricles, both surfaces with long brown hairs; lateral veins repeatedly forked, veinlets free or occasionally anastomosing near the margin to form narrow reticulate areoles. Sori borne along the lateral veins, covered by soft hairs. Odor faint, taste bitter.
Effects of Baiducao (Bai Du Cao)
Actions
The rhizome or whole herb of Ear-leaved Golden-hair Bracken (Er ye jin mao luo jue). Mainly used for wind-toxin sores and itching, eczema, and vaginal discharge.
Indications
Detoxify, dry dampness and relieve itching. Primarily for wind-toxin sores and itching, eczema, and vaginal discharge.
Usage and dosage
Internal: decoction, rhizome 9–15 g.
External: whole herb as appropriate, decocted for washing.

Cultivation and Processing of Baical Skullcap (Huang Qin)
Source
The root of the Lamiaceae plant Scutellaria baicalensis (Baical Skullcap). Harvest from spring to early summer (autumn also possible). Select plants grown 3–4 years. After digging up the roots remove stems, lateral roots and soil; when half-dry beat off the corky bark, then sun-dry to complete dryness.
Taste and Properties
Bitter, cold.
Preparation
1. Huang Qin (Baical Skullcap): pick out impurities, remove remaining stems, soak in cold water or briefly blanch in boiling water and take out; after fully moistening, slice and sun-dry (avoid excessive exposure causing reddening).
2. Wine-Processed Huang Qin: take Huang Qin slices, spray with yellow rice wine (huang jiu), mix evenly, lightly stir-fry over low heat, remove and cool to dry. (For every 100 jin [approx. 50 kg] of Huang Qin use 10–15 jin [approx. 5–7.5 kg] yellow rice wine.)
3. Stir-Fried Huang Qin: stir-fry Huang Qin slices over low heat until surface slightly charred, remove and cool.
4. Charred Huang Qin (Huang Qin Tan): stir-fry slices over high heat until surface dark brown and edges blackened while retaining medicinal properties, sprinkle with water, remove and sun-dry.
Characteristics
Dried roots are obconical, twisted and not straight, 7–27 centimeters long, diameter about 1–2 centimeters. Surface deep yellow or yellow-brown. Upper bark is coarser with twisted longitudinal wrinkles or irregular net-like lines; lower bark finer with grain or fine wrinkles; both ends have sparse wart-like lateral root scars. Texture is hard and brittle, breaks easily; cross-section deep yellow with a brown-red central pith. Old roots have a central dark brown or brown-black decayed flake in the cross-section, commonly called withered baical skullcap; roots that are hollow and not firm and split-like are commonly called baical skullcap segments. Roots turn yellow-green when wet or in cold water. Odorless, bitter taste. Best quality are long, thick, solid, yellow and cleaned of outer bark. Short, loose, deep-yellow roots that form segments are inferior. Main production areas are Hebei, Inner Mongolia, Shanxi, Shandong and Shaanxi; also produced in Liaoning and Heilongjiang.
Huang Qin produced in Sichuan and Yunnan is the root of the plant Scutellaria yunnanensis (Dian Huang Qin). The medicinal appearance is similar but thinner, diameter generally about 0.5–1.0 centimeter, often branched, cross-section a distinct yellow-green, and of lesser quality.
Effects of Baical Skullcap (Huang Qin)
Actions
The root of the Lamiaceae plant Scutellaria baicalensis (Baical Skullcap).
Main indications are clearing exuberant heat and alleviating thirst, lung-heat cough, damp-heat dysentery, jaundice, hot painful urinary dribbling, vomiting, epistaxis, uterine bleeding and leakage, red swollen painful eyes, restless fetus, and suppurative swellings and sores.
Channels
Enters the Lung, Gallbladder, Spleen, Large Intestine and Small Intestine meridians.
Indications
Drains excess fire, clears damp-heat, stops bleeding, and calms the fetus. Treats high fever with irritability and thirst, lung-heat cough, damp-heat dysentery, jaundice, heat strangury, vomiting, epistaxis, metrorrhagia and leucorrhea, red swollen painful eyes, restless fetus, and carbuncles and sores.
1. Ben Jing: treats febrile jaundice, intestinal dysentery, diarrhea, promotes urination to eliminate water retention, bleeding below and amenorrhea, treats malignant sores, ulceration and fire ulcers.
2. Bie Lu: treats phlegm-heat, stomach heat, lower abdominal colic, aids digestion, benefits the small intestine, female amenorrhea, dribbling and vaginal bleeding, and infant abdominal pain.
3. Tao Hongjing: treats ben tun (a disorder of surging pain) and heat pain below the navel.
4. Yao Xing Lun: can treat heat toxin, steaming bone disorder, alternating chills and fever, impaired digestion, breaks qi stagnation, treats five kinds of strangury, promotes free discharge, relieves joint vexation, relieves feverish thirst, treats heat abdominal masses and pain, and hardness/distention of chest and abdomen.
5. Ri Hua Zi Ben Cao: descends qi, treats epidemic febrile diseases and sores, promotes pus discharge; treats mastitis and back eruptions.
6. Zhen Zhu Nang: reduces excess yang, cools the heart and clears heat, and unblocks cold constraint.
7. Li Gao: treats fever with bitter taste in the mouth.
8. Dian Nan Ben Cao: drains lung fire upward and bladder fire downward; treats male urinary strangury, sudden uterine bleeding, regulates menstruation and clears heat, calms fetal unrest due to heat, clears fetal heat, and removes solid excess fire in the six channels.
9. Ben Cao Gang Mu: treats wind-heat and damp-heat headaches, ben tun heat pain, fiery cough, pulmonary consumption with foul throat, and various hemorrhages.
10. Ben Cao Zheng: the withered type clears upper-jiao fire, dissolves phlegm and promotes qi, calms asthma and cough, stops bleeding, relieves alternating chills and fever, wind-heat and damp-heat, headaches, resolves pestilence, clears the throat, treats pulmonary consumption and lung abscess, mastitis and back eruptions; especially expels superficial heat and so treats measles, scrofula, ulcers and red eye. The fresh/raw type cools lower-jiao heat and can treat dysentery, bladder heat accumulation, painful urinary retention, large intestine obstruction, bloody stools and uterine bleeding.
11. Scientific Folk Herbs: external washing of wounds has antiseptic action.
Dosage and Administration
Internal: decoction, 3–9 g; or used in pills or powders.
External: appropriate amount decocted for washing; or ground to powder and applied topically.
Precautions and Contraindications
Ben Cao Jing Shu: contraindicated in spleen and lung deficiency-heat.
Contraindicated in cases of middle-jiao cold causing diarrhea, cold abdominal pain, lower abdominal pain due to liver and kidney deficiency, abdominal pain from blood deficiency, spleen-deficiency diarrhea, kidney-deficiency loose stools, spleen-deficiency edema, amenorrhea from blood depletion, qi-deficiency with impaired urination, lung invaded by cold causing wheezing and cough, fetal restlessness from blood deficiency, and yin-deficiency leucorrhea.
Formulas using Baical Skullcap (Huang Qin)
1. For infant heart-heat causing terror crying: Huang Qin (remove black core) and Ginseng (Ren Shen) each one fen. Pound and sift into powder. Each dose one small scoop, take with bamboo leaf decoction at any time. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu: Huang Qin Powder)
2. To drain lung fire and reduce heat phlegm above the diaphragm: Huang Qin slices, stir-fry, make into powder, bind into paste or steam cakes the size of a wutong seed. Take fifty pills. (Danxi Xin Fa: Qing Jin Wan)
3. For chronic bronchitis: Huang Qin and Ting Li Zi (Ting Li Zi) equal parts, finely powdered, sugar-coated into tablets, each tablet contains 0.8 g of crude drug; three times daily, five tablets each time. (Inner Mongolia: Selected New Methods of Traditional Chinese Herbal Medicine)
4. For upper respiratory infection and enteritis: chop Huang Qin, soak in four times the water for four hours, strain off residue, then add twice the water and soak twice more, combine filtrates, add 20% alum solution and adjust pH to 3.5 (per 100 kg Huang Qin use 6–8 kg alum), a yellow precipitate forms, stand four hours, discard supernatant, place precipitate in cloth bag, wash with water and filter, dry, pulverize, granulate and tablet. Take two to three tablets per dose. (Liaoning: Selected New Methods of Traditional Chinese Herbal Medicine)
5. For Shaoyang and Taiyang headaches regardless of side: Huang Qin slices soaked in wine, sun-dried and powdered. Each dose one qian (approx. 3 g), take with tea or wine. (Lan Shi Mi Cang: Xiao Qing Kong Gao)
6. For combined Taiyang and Shaoyang disease with downward diarrhea: Huang Qin three liang, White Peony Root (Bai Shao) two liang, Licorice (Gan Cao, roasted) two liang, Jujube/Chinese Date (Da Zao) twelve pieces (cracked); decoct one dou of water to obtain three sheng, remove dregs. Warmly take one sheng twice daily. (Shang Han Lun: Huang Qin Tang)
7. For strangury and also to promote downward bleeding: Huang Qin four liang, finely cut, decoct in five sheng of water to obtain two sheng, divide into three doses. (Qian Jin Yi Fang)
8. For hematemesis or epistaxis, intermittent or continuous, caused by accumulated heart heat: Huang Qin one liang (remove black core), pound into fine powder. Each dose three qian, decoct in one medium cup of water to reduce to 60% volume. Take warm regardless of time. (Sheng Hui Fang: Huang Qin Powder)
9. For uterine bleeding and downward hemorrhage: Huang Qin ground to fine powder. Each dose one qian, moisten with heated scale-weights and take with wine. (Ben Shi Fang)
10. For women after age forty-nine with remaining menses or excessive continuous bleeding: Huang Qin heart-branch twigs two liang (soaked heavily in rice vinegar for seven days, dry-roasted, repeat soaking and roasting seven times). Powder finely, form vinegar pills the size of a wutong seed. Each dose seventy pills with warm wine on an empty stomach, twice daily. (Rui Zhu Tang: Qin Xin Wan)
11. For fetal fever and restlessness: Huang Qin and Atractylodes (Bai Zhu) equal parts, lightly stir-fry, powder, make honey pills the size of a wutong seed; take three qian each morning and evening with plain water. (Danxi Zuan Yao)
12. For hepatic heat producing corneal films, adults and children: Huang Qin one liang, Fresh Fermented Soybean (Dan Dou Chi) three liang, powder. Each dose three qian; wrap in cooked pig liver and eat, take with warm broth twice daily. Avoid alcohol and wheat flour. (Wei Sheng Jia Bao Fang)
13. For orbital pain due to wind-heat and phlegm: Huang Qin (wine-soaked, stir-fried) and Bai Zhi (Angelica dahurica) powdered, mix with clear tea, two qian per dose. (Danxi Xin Fa)
14. For bleeding from moxibustion sores: wine-fried Huang Qin two qian, powder, take with wine. (Guai Zheng Qi Fang)
15. For fire carbuncle: pound Huang Qin to powder, mix with water and apply topically. (Mei Shi Ji Yan Fang)
16. For postpartum intense thirst and unending drinking: Huang Qin (dried baked on new tile) and Ophiopogon (Mai Dong, core removed) each half liang.
17. For hot phlegm that is red, sticky like glue and hard, with vexation, heart pain, dry mouth and lips, inappropriate laughing and a flooding pulse: Tian Nan Xing (Arisaema), Ban Xia (Pinellia) and Huang Qin equal parts. Powder finely, soak in ginger juice, steam into cakes and form pills. Each dose 40–50 pills. (Za Bing Yuan Liu Xi Zhu: Ban Xia Wan)
18. For phlegm-heat cough with abundant qi and panting: Huang Qin three qian, charred Gardenia (Zhi Zi) and Perilla Seed (Zi Su Zi) each 1.5 qian, Poria (Fu Ling) and Bitter Apricot Kernel (Ku Xing Ren) each one qian. Decoction. (Ben Cao Hui Yan)
19. For pulmonary tidal fever and cough: Huang Qin and Salvia Root (Dan Shen) each 9–22 g, Bai Bu 12–18 g. Decoction; tablets or pills are convenient for long-term use. (Shanghai College of Traditional Chinese Medicine: Fang Ji Xue, Qin Bu Dan)
20. For febrile disease with vexation like fire, delirium and attempt to escape: Huang Qin one liang, Kansui (Gan Sui) one liang (baked until yellow), Gentian (Long Dan Cao) one liang (remove basal stalks). Pound into fine powder, each dose one qian mixed with warm water; shortly after have patient drink three liang of water to induce vomiting when the abdomen is full. Very effective for acute heat disorders. (Sheng Hui Fang)
21. For early febrile disease with agitation, headache and pain in the loins and legs: Huang Qin two fen, Fresh Ginger (Sheng Jiang) one fen, fresh Rehmannia juice three he, white honey half spoon. Decoction: simmer the first two and strain, add the latter two and boil two to three times, divide into two doses. (Sheng Hui Fang: Jie Du Yin Zi)
22. For Taiyang pattern with heavy lumbar and head pain, whole-body bone pain, short red urine, chills starting at the back, alternating chills and fever with difficult cessation of sweating: Qiang Huo (Notopterygium), Huang Qin, Chen Pi (Citrus Peel), Qian Hu (Peucedanum), Zhu Ling (Polyporus), Licorice (Gan Cao) and Anemarrhena (Zhi Mu). Decoction. (Za Bing Yuan Liu Xi Zhu: Qiang Huo Huang Qin Tang)
23. For stomach-channel heat with gum swelling and bleeding that will not ascend: Huang Qin, Coptis (Huang Lian), Raw Rehmannia (Sheng Di Huang), Moutan Bark (Mu Dan Pi), Cimicifuga (Sheng Ma) and Gypsum (Shi Gao) each one qian. Decoction, take after meals. (Wai Ke Zheng Zong: Qing Wei San)
24. For cold-damage toxic qi attacking the eyes with painful red corneal opacity: Huang Qin, Coptis (Huang Lian), Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi), Bupleurum (Chai Hu) and Scrophularia (Xuan Shen) each one liang. Grind to powder, each dose five qian; add 3–7 bamboo leaves and decoct. (Sheng Hui Fang: Huang Qin Powder)
25. For pterygium (fleshy encroachment on the eye): Huang Qin, Rhubarb (Da Huang), Saposhnikovia (Fang Feng) and Mint (Bo He) equal parts. Decoction in water, add a little honey, take after meals. (Zheng Zhi Zhun Sheng: Er Huang San)
26. For jaundice with yellow face and body and bone/joint pain due to damp-heat: Huang Qin, Qin Jiao (Qin Jiao), charred Gardenia (Zhi Zi) and Mint each two qian, Yin Chen (Artemisia capillaris) three qian. Decoction. (Ben Cao Hui Yan)
27. For cold-damage six to seven days with unresolved sweating, retching and diarrhea, difficult urination, fullness and obstruction of chest and hypochondria, low fever and vexation: Huang Qin and Cinnamon (Rou Gui) each three liang, Poria (Fu Ling) four liang, Qian Hu eight liang, Ban Xia half sheng. Decoction divided into six doses (three by day and three by night). (Wai Tai: Huang Qin Tang)
28. For upper heat and lower cold with alternating cold and heat and immediate vomiting after eating: Dried Ginger (Gan Jiang), Huang Qin, Coptis (Huang Lian) and Ginseng (Ren Shen) each three liang. Decoction, remove dregs, take in two doses. (Shang Han Lun: Gan Jiang Huang Qin Huang Lian Ren Shen Tang)
29. For liver-channel wind-heat and bleeding disorders such as uterine bleeding, bloody stools and hematuria: charred Huang Qin and Fang Feng equal parts, powdered finely, make wine pills the size of a wutong seed. Each dose 30–50 pills, take on an empty stomach or before meals with rice soup or warm wine. (Jing Yue Quan Shu: Fang Feng Huang Qin Wan)
30. For alcohol toxin with large-intestine heat accumulation and lower bleeding: Huang Qin and Fang Feng two liang each, Huang Lian four liang (half raw, half wine-fried). Powder and make vinegar pills the size of a wutong seed; take 70–80 pills on an empty stomach with rice beverage. (Jing Yue Quan Shu: Ju Jin Wan)
31. For women with excessive menstrual flow risking massive hemorrhage: Huang Qin one qian (wine-fried), Phellodendron (Huang Bai) one qian (charred), Cyperus (Xiang Fu) 1.5 qian (soaked in infant urine), White Peony Root (Bai Shao) one qian, Turtle Shell (Gui Ban) two qian (fried with fat), stink chuntree bark (Chun gen pi) two qian, local Artemisia leaf (Tu Ai Ye) one qian (fried). No adjuvant; decoct and take. (Dian Nan Ben Cao)
32. For male deficiency from excessive labor, wasting and thirst with no flesh, female leukorrhea, and alternating hot-cold in hands and feet: seasonal formulas — Spring (three months): Huang Qin and Huang Lian four liang each, Da Huang three liang; Summer: Huang Qin six liang, Huang Lian seven liang, Da Huang one liang; Autumn: Huang Qin six liang, Huang Lian three liang, Da Huang two liang; Winter: Huang Qin three liang, Da Huang five liang, Huang Lian two liang. Powder finely, make honey pills the size of a soybean, take five to seven pills three times daily. (Qian Jin Yao Fang: San Huang Wan)
33. For seminal emission with heat: Huang Qin to drain lung fire, Huang Bai to reduce yin fire, Da Huang to purge Yangming damp-heat. Powder and make honey pills the size of a wutong seed; take 50–60 pills with plain soup. (Gu Jin Yi Jian: San Huang Wan)
34. For gu-toxin dysentery resembling goose or duck liver with unbearable abdominal pain: Huang Qin (remove black core) and Huang Lian (remove rootlets, fry) each half liang. Finely chop both, decoct two cups water to one cup, remove dregs, take on an empty stomach in the evening while hot (do not take once cold as it congeals). (Sheng Ji Zong Lu: Huang Qin Tang)
35. For scrotal ulceration and exposed prolapsed testicle: Huang Lian six fen, Huang Qin, Dang Gui tail, Lian Qiao each 1.5 qian, Mu Tong and Licorice (Gan Cao) each one qian. Decoction. (Wai Ke Quan Sheng Ji: Xie Re Tang)
36. For oral sores: Huang Qin one fen, Galla (Wu Bei Zi) one fen, Toad Venom (Chan Su) half fen. Pound and sift into powder, make honey pills about the size of a small seed, take one pill and hold in the mouth to dissolve saliva until healed. (Sheng Hui Fang)
37. For residual toxicity after sweating with cheek swelling and pain: Huang Qin, Trichosanthes fruit (Gua Lou) and Licorice (Gan Cao). Crush, chew and decoct half liang per dose in plain water. (Pu Ji Fang)
38. For vitiligo (white leprosy): apply Huang Qin powder with the eggplant calyx as an applicator. (Ren Shu Bian Lan)

Banana Peel (Da Jiao Pi)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E5%A4%A7%E8%95%89%E7%9A%AE
Name
Pericarp of Common Banana (Da Jiao Pi)
Banana Peel (Xiang Jiao Pi)
Cultivation and Preparation of Pericarp of Common Banana (Da Jiao Pi)
Source
It is the pericarp of Musaceae plants such as Common Banana (Da Jiao). The banana peels are collected in autumn and sun-dried.
Morphology
1. Common Banana (Da Jiao), a perennial tufted herb, 3–7 m tall. It has stolons; the pseudostem is thick and heavy, somewhat covered with bloom. Petioles are very long, over 30 cm, often with bloom, with closed leaf wings; leaves erect or held upward, long-elliptic, 1.5–3 m long and 40–60 cm wide, adaxial surface dark green, abaxial surface pale green and conspicuously covered with bloom, base nearly cordate or auriculate and nearly symmetrical, apex acute or acuminate. The spike-like inflorescence is pendulous, rachis glabrous, bracts ovate or ovate-lanceolate, 15–30 cm or longer, deciduous, outer surface purplish-red, inner surface deep red, each bract with two rows of flowers, staminate flowers falling off; perianth pale yellow-white, fused perianth lobes 4–6.5 cm long, free perianth lobes about half the length of the fused lobes, translucent and waxy with luster, oblong or nearly circular, apex with a small mucro, acuminate or rolled into a pouch. The infructescence consists of 7–8 tiers to several dozen tiers of fruit clusters. Fruits oblong, relatively short and stout in length-to-width ratio, body straight or slightly curved, 10–20 cm long, with distinct edges, pedicel usually elongated, flesh fine and firm, astringent before ripening, sweet or slightly sour at maturity but lacking aroma or only slightly aromatic, seedless or with few seeds. Flowering and fruiting occur year-round.
2. Banana (Xiang Jiao), a perennial herb with stolons. Plants are tufted, generally less than 2 m tall, with tall types reaching 4–5 m. Pseudostems are uniformly dark green with black spots and covered with bloom, especially in the upper parts. Petioles short and thick, usually less than 30 cm long, leaf-wing obvious and open, margins brown-red or bright red. Leaf blades long-elliptic, length (1.5–)2–2.2 m, width 60–70 cm, apex obtuse-rounded, base nearly rounded and symmetrical, adaxial surface dark green without bloom, abaxial surface pale green with bloom. Inflorescence pendulous, rachis densely covered with brown pubescence, bract outer surface dark purple, male flower bracts not deciduous, each bract enclosing two rows of flowers; flowers milk-white or slightly pale purple, free perianth lobes nearly circular and entire, apex with an acutely conical tip, the fused perianth bears two small lateral lobes about half the length of the central lobe. The largest bunches may have up to 360 fruits, weighing up to 32 kg; ordinary bunches have 8–10 tiers with 150–200 fruits; fruits oblong, 15–25 cm long, with distinct ridges of 4–5 angles, apex gradually narrowed, peduncle short, peel green, flesh sweet and smooth, seedless, very fragrant. Flowering and fruiting occur year-round.
Habitat and Distribution
1. In China, Fujian, Taiwan, Guangdong, Guangxi and Yunnan all cultivate it. Native to India, Malaysia and other places.
2. Native to southern China. Cultivated in Fujian, Taiwan, Guangdong, Guangxi and Yunnan.
Nature and Flavor
Flavor sweet; astringent; nature cold
Physical Characteristics
Pericarp: fresh is yellow-green, dried is dark brown, appearing as irregular strips and pieces, soft yet tough, with many fibers; bears a relatively long pedicel whose fibers are strong, about 4–5 cm long. The dried, clean specimens are preferred.
Effects of Pericarp of Common Banana (Da Jiao Pi)
Efficacy
It is the pericarp of Musaceae plants such as Common Banana (Da Jiao). Main indications are dysentery, cholera, skin itching, and hypertension.
Indications
Clears heat and detoxifies, lowers blood pressure. Mainly for dysentery, cholera, skin itching, and hypertension.
Dosage and Administration
Internal: decoction, 30–60 g.
External: decoct an appropriate amount for washing; or grind to powder and apply topically.
Discussions by Various Authors
Guangdong Chinese Materia Medica: orally used to treat dysentery. Frying then decocting and drinking treats cholera abdominal pain. Decoction for washing treats skin itching.
Prescriptions of Pericarp of Common Banana (Da Jiao Pi)
For treating nasal ulcers (painful ulcers inside the nasal cavity): Sweet Banana pericarp (Gan Jiao Pi) dried, baked and ground into a fine powder, mixed
Borneol (Bing Pian)
, Tea Seed Oil (Cha You)
and applied to the affected area. (Quanzhou Materia Medica)
