Buddleja officinalis (Mi Meng Hua)
Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E5%AF%86%E8%92%99%E8%8A%B1
Name
Butterfly-bush Flower
Menghua (Meng Hua), Menghuazhu (Meng Hua Zhu), Laomenghua (Lao Meng Hua), Yangerduo Duojian (Yang Er Duo Duo Jian), Shuijin Flower (Shui Jin Hua), Yellow-flowered Zuiyucao (Huang Hua Zui Yu Cao)
Menghua (Meng Hua)
Menghuazhu (Meng Hua Zhu)
Laomenghua (Lao Meng Hua)
Yangerduo Duojian (Yang Er Duo Duo Jian)
Shuijin Flower (Shui Jin Hua)
Yellow-flowered Zuiyucao (Huang Hua Zui Yu Cao)
Huangfan Flower (Huang Fan Hua)
Small Brocade Flower (Xiao Jin Hua)
Cultivation and Processing of Butterfly-bush Flower
Source
The dried flowers or flower buds of Mimenghua, a plant of the Loganiaceae family. Clustered flower buds are picked before opening between February and March, stems and impurities removed, then sun-dried.
Properties and Taste
Sweet, cold.
Processing
Pick out impurities and sieve off ash and soil.
Description
An inflorescence of many small clustered buds. Shape and size vary, surface gray-yellow or light brown, densely covered with downy hairs. Single bud short rod-shaped, thicker at the top and thinner at the base, 3–6 mm long, apex rounded and slightly swollen; calyx bell-shaped, four-cleft; corolla tubular, lobes dark purple, hairs very sparse. Whole material soft and brittle, cross-section black in the center. Slight fragrance; sweet with a slight bitter, pungent note. Best quality when buds are densely clustered, gray-yellow, hairy and soft in texture.
Effects of Butterfly-bush Flower
Functions
The dried flowers or flower buds of Mimenghua, a plant of the Loganiaceae family.
Indications: red swollen painful eyes, excessive tearing and photophobia, dim vision and corneal opacities, wind-strung ulcerating eyes.
Channels
Wang Haogu: enters the Liver meridian.
Main Actions
Expels wind, cools the blood, moistens the Liver and clears the eyes. Treats red swollen painful eyes, excessive tearing and photophobia, dim vision and corneal opacities, wind-strung ulcerating eyes.
Clears the Liver and brightens the eyes: this herb is a specialist for ophthalmic disorders. For eye disease due to blood deficiency with Liver heat it is often combined with Goji Berry (Gou Qi Zi) and Cuscuta Seed (Tu Si Zi). For eye disease due to excess heat in the Liver meridian it is often combined with Qing Xiang Seed (Qing Xiang Zi) and Chrysanthemum Flower (Ju Hua).
Usage and Dosage
Internal use: decoct 3–9 g; or used in pills or powders.
Formulas of Butterfly-bush Flower
1. For wind invasion with eye symptoms—dimmed vision, sticky tears and photophobia, eyelids with wind papules, gritty obstruction difficult to open, itching or pain, gradually forming a veil membrane with unclear vision, chronic unilateral headache drawing the eyes with progressive reduction in visual acuity, dullness and aching, and sudden red swollen pain: Butterfly-bush Flower (cleaned) (Mi Meng Hua), Abalone Shell (Shi Jue Ming) (boiled with salt in running water for one fu period then filtered and ground to powder), Horsetail (Mu Zei), Tribulus (Ji Li) (stir-fried to remove spines), Notopterygium (Qiang Huo) (remove stems), Chrysanthemum Flower (Ju Hua), equal parts. Grind to a fine powder; each dose one qian, taken with preserved tea (la cha) after meals, twice daily. (Bureau Prescription: Mimenghua Powder)
2. For corneal opacity and eye opacities: Butterfly-bush Flower (Mi Meng Hua) and Phellodendron Bark root (Huang Bai) (washed and scraped) one liang each. Pound and sift into a powder, bind with honey into pills about the size of a parasol-tree seed; each dose ten to fifteen pills after meals, taken at bedtime with warm water, or taken with a decoction sweetened with maltose. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu: Mimenghua Pills)
3. For photophobia and blurred vision due to Liver and Gallbladder deficiency: Butterfly-bush Flower (Mi Meng Hua), Notopterygium (Qiang Huo), Chrysanthemum Flower (Ju Hua), Vitex Fruit (Man Jing Zi), Qing Xiang Seed (Qing Xiang Zi), Horsetail (Mu Zei), Abalone Shell (Shi Jue Ming), Tribulus (Ji Li), Goji Berry (Gou Qi Zi), equal parts. Grind to a powder; each dose three qian, taken after meals with clear tea. (Yin Hai Jing Wei: Mimenghua Powder)
4. For aversion to light and photophobia of the eyes: Butterfly-bush Flower 3 qian, Raw Rehmannia Root (Sheng Di Huang) 2 qian, Scutellaria (Huang Qin) 2 qian. Decoction.
5. For ulceration and damp-rot of the eyelid with excessive tearing: Butterfly-bush Flower 3 qian, Atractylodes (Bai Zhu) 2 qian, Solomon's Seal (Yu Zhu) 5 qian. Decoction. (Formulas 4–5 from Ben Cao Hui Yan)
6. For pediatric malnutrition with attacking eyes and impending blindness: Butterfly-bush Flower one liang, Quisqualis Fruit kernel (Shi Jun Zi rou) 3 qian, White Wuyi (Bai Wu Yi) 5 qian, Picrasma (Hu Huang Lian) 2 qian, Aloe (Lu Hui) 1 qian. Grind together and bind with sugar into pills the size of a chickpea; one pill each morning and evening, taken down with warm water.
7. For all chronic eye disorders from prolonged strain with one eye dominant, causing fatigue of the eye, producing a feeling of swelling, pain and blurred vision: Butterfly-bush Flower 5 qian, Sweet Chrysanthemum (Gan Ju Hua) 2 qian, Ophiopogon (Mai Dong) (heart removed) 8 qian, Angelica sinensis (Dang Gui) 1 qian 5 fen, Solomon's Seal (Yu Zhu) 4 qian. Decoction. (Formulas 6–7 from Ben Cao Hui Yan)
8. For Liver deficiency and decreased visual acuity: Butterfly-bush Flower 12 g, Goji Berry (Gou Qi Zi) 12 g, Chrysanthemum Flower (Ju Hua) 12 g, Raw Rehmannia Root (Sheng Di Huang) 12 g, Chu Shi Seed (Chu Shi Zi) 12 g, Quince (Mu Gua) 6 g, Cortex Fraxini (Qin Pi) 6 g. Roll with honey into pills; each dose 9 g, taken three times daily. (Sichuan Materia Medica, 1982)
9. For night blindness: Butterfly-bush Flower 15 g, Qing Xiang Seed (Qing Xiang Zi) 15 g, Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) 12 g. Grind finely, stuff into pig liver and cook until done then dry and bake, add Plantain Seed (Che Qian Zi), Cuttlebone (Hai Piao Xiao) and Yeming Sha (Yeming Sha) 9 g each, mix to a fine powder; take 9 g morning and evening with warm water, for three consecutive doses. (Gansu TCM Effective Prescriptions Collection)
10. For dizziness: steam Butterfly-bush Flower with a small chicken, strain off dregs and take the soup and meat. (Miao Ethnic Medicine Collection)
11. For pertussis (whooping cough): use Yangerduo Duojian steamed with rice soup oil, honey or sugar; alternatively stuff Yangerduo Duojian into peeled, cored pearl pears, add honey and steam. (Kunming Common Folk Herbs)

Cultivation and Processing of Bupleurum (Chai Hu)
Source
This item is the dried root of Umbelliferae plants Bupleurum chinense DC. (Bupleurum (Chai Hu)) or narrow‑leaved Bupleurum Bupleurum scorzonerifolium Willd. (Narrow‑leaved Bupleurum (Xia Ye Chai Hu)). According to differing characteristics they are commonly called northern Bupleurum and southern Bupleurum. Harvested in spring and autumn, remove stems, leaves and mud and sand, then dry.
Properties and Flavor
Bitter, slightly cold.
Processing
1. Bupleurum (Chai Hu): remove impurities, remove residual stems, wash clean of mud and sand, lift out, moisten thoroughly then promptly slice, and immediately sun‑dry.
2. Vinegar‑processed Bupleurum: take Bupleurum slices, mix evenly with vinegar, place in a pot and stir‑fry over low heat until the vinegar is absorbed and slightly dry, remove and sun‑dry. (For every 100 jin of Bupleurum, use 12 jin of vinegar.)
3. Turtle‑blood Bupleurum: take Bupleurum slices, place in a large basin, pour in turtle blood slightly diluted with warm water, mix evenly, macerate until moistened, place in a pot and lightly stir‑fry over low heat, remove and cool. (For every 100 jin of Bupleurum, use blood from 200 live turtles.)
4. Wine‑processed Bupleurum: take Bupleurum slices, mix evenly with yellow wine, macerate until thoroughly moistened, place in a pot and heat over low fire to stir‑fry until dry, remove and cool. (For every 100 kg of Bupleurum slices, use 10 kg of yellow wine.)
5. Charred Bupleurum: take Bupleurum slices, stir‑fry over low heat until the exterior is black and the interior brownish, spray in a small amount of water, remove and air‑dry.
6. Honey‑processed Bupleurum: put honey into a pot, heat until boiling, pour in Bupleurum slices, stir‑fry over low heat until deep yellow and not sticky to the touch.
Description
Northern Bupleurum (Bei Chai Hu): cylindrical or long conical in shape, length 6–15 cm, diameter 0.3–0.8 cm. Root crown swollen, apex retaining 3–15 stem bases or short fibrous leaf bases, branches in the lower part. Surface dark brown or light brown, with longitudinal wrinkles, lateral root scars and lenticels. Texture hard and tough, not easy to break; fracture shows fibrous nature, cortex light brown, wood portion yellowish‑white. Slight aromatic odor, slightly bitter taste.
Southern Bupleurum (Nan Chai Hu): roots thinner, conical, apex with many fine hair‑like withered leaf fibers, lower part mostly unbranched or slightly branched. Surface reddish‑brown or dark brown, near the root crown often with dense annular rings. Texture somewhat soft, easy to break, fracture surface slightly flat, not showing fibrous nature. Has rancid oily odor.
Effects of Bupleurum (Chai Hu)
Actions
This product is the dried root of Bupleurum or narrow‑leaved Bupleurum (Umbelliferae).
Indications
Mainly for alternating chills and fever, chest fullness and hypochondriac pain, bitter taste in the mouth and deafness, headache and vertigo, malaria, diarrhea and rectal prolapse, irregular menses, uterine prolapse.
Channels
Enter
Liver Channel,
Gallbladder Channel.
Indications
Harmonizes the exterior and interior, spreads the Liver, raises yang. Treats alternating chills and fever, chest fullness and hypochondriac pain, bitter taste and deafness, headache and vertigo, malaria, diarrhea and rectal prolapse, irregular menses, uterine prolapse.
① Ben Jing: Governs qi accumulation in the heart, abdomen and stomach, food stagnation, pathogenic cold and heat, promotes discharge of the old and generation of the new.
② Bie Lu: Dispels vexation and heat below the heart from cold damage, resolves various phlegm‑heat accumulations, counterflow in the chest, wandering qi among the five viscera, large intestine stagnation, edema, and damp‑bi with cramping. Can also be used as a bathing decoction.
③ Yao Xing Lun: Treats summer‑heat and bone‑and‑joint vexing pain, heat qi, shoulder and back pain, promotes circulation of blood and qi, fatigue and emaciation; promotes descending qi and digestion, indicated for epidemic febrile diseases unresolved internally or externally, decocted alone.
④ Qian Jin Fang: Sprout juice treats deafness, used to irrigate the ear.
⑤ Si Sheng Ben Cao: Indicated for copious phlegm and for masses and fullness in the chest and hypochondria.
⑥ Ri Hua Zi Ben Cao: Tonifies the five fatigues and seven injuries, relieves vexation and fright, augments qi and strength, transforms phlegm and stops cough, moistens heart and lungs, replenishes essence and marrow, for febrile diseases with heat, mania and collapse, chest and hypochondrial fullness, and forgetfulness.
⑦ Zhen Zhu Nang: Eliminates alternating chills and fever and gallbladder bi; only Bupleurum shoots can remove it.
⑧ Yi Xue Qi Yuan: Eliminates deficiency vexation and heat, disperses muscular heat, removes morning tidal fever.
⑨ Dian Nan Ben Cao: An essential drug for inducing sweat to release the exterior in cold damage, clears pathogenic heat circulating in the six channels, treats paralysis and atrophy, removes pathogenic heat of the Liver system and consumptive fever, moves constrained Liver‑channel qi, relieves left hypochondriac pain from Liver qi, treats women’s blood‑heat burning during menses and regulates menses. Use young flower buds for inducing sweat; use the root to treat deficiency heat and regulate menses.
⑩ Ben Cao Gang Mu (Compendium of Materia Medica): Treats sinking yang qi, pacifies Liver, Gallbladder, Sanjiao and pericardial fire, and headaches, vertigo, dim or red painful eyes with obstructions, deafness and tinnitus, various malarias, alternating cold and heat from phlegmatic dampness, women’s heat entering the blood chamber and irregular menses, residual heat after pediatric smallpox, and wasting disorders.
Usage and Dosage
Internal: decoction, 3–10 g; or in pills or powders.
External: appropriate amount, decoct for washing; or grind to powder and apply as a poultice.
Precautions and Contraindications
Contraindicated in true yin deficiency and ascendant Liver yang.
① Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu: Pinellia (Ban Xia) acts as its assistant. Antagonistic to Gleditsia (Zao Jiao). Avoid with Inula (Nu Wan) and Veratrum (Li Lu).
② Yi Xue Ru Men: In cases of exhausted original qi or yin deficit with profuse sweating, mistaken ingestion can be fatal.
③ Ben Cao Jing Shu: Contraindicated in patients who are deficient with rebellious qi rising, in vomiting, and in yin deficiency with blazing fire ascending; same as the classical rules. Do not take for malaria that is not of the Shaoyang channel.

① For cold damage on the fifth or sixth day, windstroke, alternating chills and fever, chest and hypochondriac fullness, wheezy reluctance to eat, vexation with desire to vomit, or vexation in the chest without vomiting, or thirst, or abdominal pain, or palpable stasis under the hypochondrium, or palpitation below the heart, difficulty urinating, or no thirst with slight fever, or cough: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) half jin,
Scutellaria (Huang Qin) 3 liang,
Ginseng (Ren Shen) 3 liang,
Pinellia (Ban Xia) half sheng (washed),
Licorice (Gan Cao) (honey‑fried),
Fresh ginger (Sheng Jiang) 3 liang each (sliced), Jujube (Da Zao) 12 pieces (split). Take the above seven ingredients with 1 dou 2 sheng of water, boil down to obtain 6 sheng, strain off dregs, then decoct to obtain 3 sheng, take warm 1 sheng, three times daily. (Shang Han Lun: Xiao Chai Hu Tang)
② For pathogenic invasion of channels and collaterals, emaciation with muscular heat, promoting discharge of the old and generation of the new; for summer diarrhea, epidemics, apoplexy, and hidden summerheat: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) 4 liang (washed, remove sprouts),
Licorice (Gan Cao) 1 liang (honey‑fried). Grind to a fine powder. Each dose 2 qian, water one gao, decoct to eight tenths and take hot after meals. (Ben Shi Fang: Chai Hu San)
③ For external wind‑cold with fever and aversion to cold, headache and body pain; early stage intermittent malaria: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) 1–3 qian,
Saposhnikovia (Fang Feng) 1 qian,
Aged tangerine peel (Chen Pi) 1.5 qian,
White Peony (Bai Shao) 2 qian,
Licorice (Gan Cao) 1 qian,
Fresh ginger (Sheng Jiang) 3–5 slices. Water 1.5 zhong, decoct to 70–80% and take hot. (Jing Yue Quan Shu: Zheng Chai Hu Yin)
④ For Liver qi: Bupleurum (Chai Hu), Aged tangerine peel (Chen Pi) each 1.2 qian,
Red Peony (Chi Shao), Bitter orange (Zhi Ke), vinegar‑fried Cyperus (Xiang Fu) each 1 qian, Honey‑fried Licorice (Gan Cao) 0.5 qian. (From Yi Yi Ou Lu: Chai Hu Shu Gan Yin)
⑤ For Liver‑channel constrained fire and internal hypochondriac pain: Bupleurum (Chai Hu), Scutellaria (Huang Qin), Gardenia (Zhi Zi), Green tangerine peel (Qing Pi), White Peony (Bai Shao), Bitter orange (Zhi Ke). (From Zheng Yin Mai Zhi: Chai Hu Qing Gan Yin)
⑥ For blood deficiency with fatigue, five‑center heat, body pain, dizziness and heaviness of head and eyes, palpitations, flushed cheeks, dry mouth and throat, low‑grade fever and night sweats, reduced appetite, desire to lie down, and blood‑heat patterns with irregular menses, umbilical and abdominal distention and pain, intermittent chills and fever like malaria; also for maidens with blood deficiency and yin deficiency, disharmony of nutrient and protective qi, chronic cough with tidal fever, emaciation gradually leading to steaming bone disorder: Licorice (Gan Cao) 0.5 liang (honey‑fried, slightly charred),
Angelica (Dang Gui) (remove sprouts, grated, lightly fried),
Poria (Fu Ling) (peeled, white portion),
White Peony (Bai Shao),
Atractylodes (Bai Zhu),
Bupleurum (Chai Hu) (remove sprouts) each 1 liang. Grind coarsely. Each dose 2 qian, water one large cup, warm a piece of fresh ginger and crush it, add a little Mint (Bo He), decoct to 70%, strain and take hot at any time. (Ju Fang: Xiao Yao San)
⑦ For night sweats and alternating chills and fever: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) (remove sprouts),
Picrorhiza or Hu Huang Lian (Hu Huang Lian) equal parts, make into fine powder, refine with honey into an ointment and form pills the size of a chickpea. Take one or two pills with a little wine dissolved in five fen of water, boil in a heavy decoction for 20–30 boils, let warm and take at no fixed time. (Pediatric Hygiene formula: Chai Hu Huang Lian Gao)
⑧ For disharmony of nutrient and protective qi, body heat and night sweats, joint and muscle pain, general fatigue and lack of strength, poor appetite and erratic eating: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) 2 liang,
Turtle shell (Bie Jia) 2 liang,
Licorice (Gan Cao),
Anemarrhena (Zhi Mu) each 1 liang,
Gentiana macrophylla (Qin Jiao) 1.5 liang. Pound the five ingredients to powder. Each dose 2 qian, water 0.8 fen, 2 jujubes, decoct to 60% and take hot. (Bo Ji Fang: Chai Hu San)
⑨ For jaundice: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) 1 liang (remove sprouts), Licorice (Gan Cao) 1 fen. Grind finely into one dose, with one bowl of water and a handful of Imperata root (Bai Mao Gen), decoct to 70%, strain off dregs, take as desired during the day, finish in one day. (Chuan Jia Mi Bao Fang)
⑩ For Liver jaundice, sallow complexion, limb stiffness, dry mouth and tongue, slurred speech, blue fingernails and toenails: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) 1 liang (remove sprouts),
Licorice (Gan Cao) 0.5 liang (honey‑fried and slightly charred, grated),
Cassia seed (Jue Ming Zi) 0.5 liang,
Plantain seed (Che Qian Zi) 10 liang, Antelope horn shavings (Ling Yang Jiao) 0.5 liang. Grind the above into a powder. Each dose 3 qian, water one medium cup, decoct to 50%, strain off dregs, take warm at any time. (Sheng Hui Fang: Chai Hu San)

Schizonepeta spikes (Jing Jie) 1 fen each. Pound these three to the size of a small bean. Bitter orange (Zhi Ke) one qu (remove awn). Grind the five into powder. Each dose 3 large qian, water 3 cups, decoct to 60%, take warm, only two doses daily, no overdose. When urination and defecation are relieved, sweating will occur spontaneously. (Bo Ji Fang: Chai Hu San)
⒂ For pregnant women with alternating chills and fever, headache, reluctance to eat, hypochondriac pain, nausea and rebellious qi; and for postpartum cold damage, heat entering the uterus, alternating chills and fever like malaria, irregular menses, convalescent lingering heat: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) 1 liang,
Scutellaria (Huang Qin),
Ginseng (Ren Shen),
Licorice (Gan Cao) (honey‑fried) each 1.5 fen. Grind to the size of a small bean. Each dose 5 qian, water 1.5 cups, decoct to one cup, strain and take. (Lei Zheng Huo Ren Shu: Huang Long Tang)

⒄ For malaria with more cold than heat and abdominal distention: Bupleurum (Chai Hu),
Pinellia (Ban Xia),
Magnolia bark (Hou Po),

Ligusticum (Chuan Xiong),
Bitter orange (Zhi Ke) (bran‑fried),

Scutellaria (Huang Qin), Hu Huang Lian (Hu Huang Lian), Aucklandia (Mu Xiang), Corydalis (Yan Hu Suo) each 10 g, Hang Bai Shao (Hang Bai Shao) 15 g, fresh Rhubarb (Da Huang) 15 g (added later), Glauber’s salt (Mang Xiao) 10 g (taken dissolved). [Dietary therapy formula]
Bupleurum (Chai Hu), White Peony (Bai Shao), and Moutan Cortex (Mu Dan Pi) stewed with lean pork
Bupleurum (Chai Hu) 6 g,
Moutan Cortex (Mu Dan Pi)
6 g,
White Peony (Bai Shao)
10 g, lean pork 30 g, seasonings as required. Wash Bupleurum (Chai Hu), Moutan Cortex (Mu Dan Pi), and White Peony (Bai Shao) and stew together with the lean pork until the meat is very tender; add seasonings to taste. Drink the broth and eat the meat.
Functions: Soothes the Liver and relieves constraint, softens the Liver and clears heat.
[Notes]
(1) For treating colds it is often used together with Kudzu Root (Ge Gen), Notopterygium (Qiang Huo), and others. Bupleurum (Chai Hu) has a relatively good antipyretic effect; when the pathogen is in the Shaoyang and chills and fever alternate, it is often combined with Scutellaria (Huang Qin) and Pinellia (Ban Xia) (for example, Xiao Chai Hu Tang); for malarial disorders Bupleurum (Chai Hu) can be paired with Tsaoko (Cao Guo) or Unripe Tangerine Peel (Qing Pi). Bupleurum (Chai Hu) has a good effect in soothing the Liver and relieving constraint and also serves as a guide among liver-dispersing medicines; it is an important drug for treating liver qi stagnation. It can be used for chest and hypochondriac pain whether caused internally by liver constraint or externally by trauma; for menstrual irregularities or dysmenorrhea caused by liver qi stagnation it can be used with Angelica (Dang Gui), White Peony (Bai Shao), Cyperus (Xiang Fu), Curcuma (Yu Jin), and other herbs. Bupleurum (Chai Hu) has an ascending and floating nature; when combined with qi-tonifying herbs such as Codonopsis (Dang Shen) and Astragalus (Huang Qi), it can raise the yang and is used for conditions such as chronic diarrhea with prolapse of the rectum and uterine prolapse due to qi deficiency and sinking.
(2) As a single medicine Bupleurum (Chai Hu) is light, clear, ascending and dispersing, and also has the function of facilitating dissemination. It can release the exterior and reduce fever, soothe the Liver and relieve constraint, and can also be used to raise yang qi. Therefore, clinically it can be used for both excess and deficiency syndromes. Different combinations allow it to exert various effects, for example: paired with Kudzu Root (Ge Gen) and Notopterygium (Qiang Huo) it induces sweating and releases the exterior; paired with Scutellaria (Huang Qin) and Artemisia annua (Qing Hao) it clears heat through the exterior; paired with Dichroa (Chang Shan) and Tsaoko (Cao Guo) it arrests malaria and reduces fever; paired with Cyperus (Xiang Fu) and Curcuma (Yu Jin) it soothes the Liver and relieves constraint; paired with Codonopsis (Dang Shen), Astragalus (Huang Qi), Atractylodes (Bai Zhu), and Cimicifuga (Sheng Ma) it raises and lifts yang qi. However, it is not suitable for those with yin deficiency and lack of fluids or with hyperactive liver yang. Bupleurum (Chai Hu) and Kudzu Root (Ge Gen) have similar light, clear, ascending and dispersing actions and are often used together to release the exterior and reduce fever, but each has its strengths: Bupleurum (Chai Hu) soothes the Liver and relieves constraint and, when combined with tonifying herbs, can raise yang to treat uterine prolapse and rectal prolapse, but it does not generate fluids or quench thirst; Kudzu Root (Ge Gen) generates fluids and relieves thirst, can raise clear yang and is used for watery diarrhea, but it does not have the function of soothing the Liver and relieving constraint.

Great Burdock Achene, Achene of Great Burdock
Eshi (Eshi), Mouse-sticky Seed (Shuzhanzi), Shu-sticky Seed (Shuzhanzi), Dali Seed (Dali Zi), Maoranran Seed (Maoranranzi), Black-wind Seed (Heifengzi), Hair-cone Seed (Maozhuizi), Sticky Cang Seed (Zhancangzi), Big Niu-le (Daniu Le), Niu Seed (Niuzi), Earth Big-tong Seed (Tu Datuanzi), Ten-thousand Hook (Wanbagou), Mouse-point Seed (Shujianzi)

Cultivation and Processing of Great Burdock Achene (Niubangzi)
Source
The fruit of the Asteraceae plant Arctium (burdock). When the fruits mature in August to September, collect in batches. Sun-dry, thresh out the fruits, remove impurities, then sun-dry until completely dry. Can be used raw or stir-fried until yellow.
Distribution
Mainly produced in Hebei; also in Jilin, Liaoning, Zhejiang, Heilongjiang and other places. In addition, Sichuan, Henan, Hubei, Shaanxi and other areas also produce it. Output is larger in the northeast, and Zhejiang products are of better quality.
Properties and Taste
Pungent and bitter, cold.
Processing
Great Burdock Achene (Niubangzi): pick out impurities and sieve off soil particles.
Stir-fried Great Burdock Achene (Chao Niubangzi): take clean Great Burdock Achenes, put them in a pan, stir-fry over low heat until slightly puffed, the outside becomes slightly yellow and emits a light fragrance, then remove and cool.
Description
The achene is oblong-ovoid, about 6 millimeters long, with a central diameter of about 3 millimeters. The pericarp is grayish-brown, with several slightly raised longitudinal ribs, one more distinct in the middle; the whole surface has sparse spots and resembles a dense network pattern. One end is slightly narrow and slightly curved, with a light-colored small dot at the apex; the other end is bluntly rounded, slightly wider, with a small pit. The longitudinal surface is somewhat prominent, the margin is smooth, rounded and thick. The pericarp is relatively hard; when broken the kernel splits into two cotyledons, gray-white and oily. Odorless, slightly bitter. The best specimens are large, full, with a grayish-brown pericarp.
Effects of Great Burdock Achene (Niubangzi)
Functions
The fruit of the Asteraceae plant Arctium (burdock).
Main indications: wind-heat cough, swollen and painful throat, rashes that fail to surface, itchy urticaria, carbuncles and sores with toxin.
Channels Entered
Enters
the Lung meridian
,
the Stomach meridian
.
Main Actions
Disperse wind-heat, open the lungs and expel rashes, reduce swelling and detoxify. Used for wind-heat cough, swollen and painful throat, rashes that fail to surface, itchy urticaria, and carbuncles and sores with toxin.
① Bielu (Bielu): brightens the eyes, tonifies the middle, dispels wind injury.
② Yaoxing Lun (On Drug Properties): dispels various wind, benefits the waist and legs, and also disperses various nodules and the vexing heat-toxin of sinews and bones.
③ Shiliao Benca o (Dietary Materia Medica): roast to powder, brew like tea three bi, promotes urination.
④ Bencao Shiyi (Supplement to Materia Medica): treats wind-toxin swellings and various atrophies.
⑤ Yixue Qiyuan (Origins of Medicine): reduces and benefits the throat and diaphragm. Zhuzhi Miyao (Secret Essentials of Indications): moistens the lungs and disperses qi.
⑥ Li Gao: treats wind-damp pruritic rashes, wind-heat of the throat, disperses the toxins of swellings and ulcers, and benefits stagnant qi in the waist and knees.
⑦ Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica): eliminates toxins of rashes.
Usage and Dosage
Internal: decoct, 5–10 g; or included in powdered formulas.
External: appropriate amount, decocted for gargling.
Precautions and Contraindications
Bencao Jingshu (Commentary on the Materia Medica): do not use recklessly in cases of qi deficiency with a pale complexion and spontaneous bowel movements or diarrhea; for carbuncles that have already suppurated, it is inappropriate to use unless there is constipation.
Formulas Containing Great Burdock Achene (Niubangzi)
① To disperse wind and relieve excessive phlegm and saliva obstructing the throat and diaphragm: Great Burdock Achene (slightly fried) (Niubangzi (Chao)), Schizonepeta spikes (Jingjie Sui) each one liang, Licorice (honey-fried) (Gancao (Zhi)) half liang. Grind to powder; after eating lie down at night; take two qian with a little decoction, action will be gradual. (Bencao Yanyi)
② Treating throat obstruction: Great Burdock Achene six fen, Ma-lian Seed eight fen. Pound the two into a powder; on an empty stomach take one warm-water measure (fangcun bi) gradually increasing to one and a half, twice daily. (Guangji Fang)
③ For wind-heat obstructing the throat with generalized edema: Great Burdock Achene one he (half raw half cooked), pound into powder, mix with hot wine and take one qian. (Jingyan Fang)
④ For wind-heat attacking the upper burner with hanging carbuncles and swelling pain: Eshi (stir-fried) and Licorice (raw) each one liang. Make into powder; each dose two qian, one cup of water, decoct to six fen, hold in the mouth for a while then swallow. (Puji Fang - Qi Guan San)
⑤ For rashes that fail to surface: finely ground Great Burdock Achene five qian, decocted Tamarix (Chengliu) and take to induce surfacing. (Bencao Huiyan)
⑥ For wind-heat skin lesions with widespread pruritic rashes: Great Burdock Achene and Duckweed (Fuping) in equal parts. Use Mint (Bohe) decoction to take two qian, twice daily. (Yangsheng Biyong Fang)
⑦ For wind-swelling with itchy toxic rashes: Great Burdock Achene, Scrophularia (Xuanshen), Stiff Silkworm (Jiangcan), and Mint (Bohe) each five qian. Make to powder; each dose three qian, take with plain decoction. (Fangmai Zhengzong)
⑧ For phlegm-induced fainting and headache: Inula Flower one liang, Great Burdock Achene one liang (lightly fried). Pound to a fine powder, mix without regard to timing, take one qian with waxed-flour tea. (Shenghui Fang)
⑨ For headache radiating to the eyes with blurred vision: Great Burdock Achene, Xanthium Fruit (Cang'erzi), Sweet Chrysanthemum (Ganju hua) each three qian. Decoction and take. (Fangmai Zhengzong)
⑩ For wind-heat turning into painful fixed joints attacking the fingers causing red swelling and numbness, possibly advancing to shoulders, back and knees, triggered by summer heat or constipation: Great Burdock Achene three liang (stir-fried between paper), Fresh fermented soybeans (Xin Douchi) (stir-fried), Notopterygium (Qianghuo) (remove reed) each one liang, dry Raw Rehmannia two liang and a half, Astragalus (Huangqi) one liang and a half (honey-fried). Grind to fine powder; take two qian with decoction on an empty stomach before meals, three times daily. (Ben Shi Fang - Niubangzi San)
⑾ For wind-heat of the head and face, or phlegm-toxin of the neck and throat, wind-heat dental carbuncle: Great Burdock Achene, Mint (Bohe), Schizonepeta (Jingjie), Gardenia (Zhizi), Moutan Cortex (Mudanpi), Dendrobium (Shihu), Scrophularia (Xuanshen), Prunella (Xiakucao); decoct in water and take. (Yangke Xinde Ji - Niubang Jieji Tang)
⑿ For wind-related toothache: stir-fried Great Burdock Achene, decoct and gargle then spit out. (Yannian Fang)
⒀ For breast distension from wind: Mouse-sticky Seed with musk and wine swallowed. (Xiuzhen Fang)
⒁ For perianal carbuncle: Mouse-sticky Seed three qian stir-fried, finely powdered, mixed with one spoon of honey and one spoon of purified niter, take with warm wine on an empty stomach. (Xiuzhen Fang)
⒂ For heat stagnation in the upper burner with sudden swelling and painful obstructed throat: Eshi (lightly fried until fragrant) one liang, Licorice (honey-fried) one fen, Schizonepeta (stems removed) half liang. Pound the three into a fine powder. Each dose two qian, five-tenths of a cup of water, decoct to a boil and take warm. Taking a few sips of boiling decoction is also acceptable. (Shengji Zonglu - Eshi San)
⒃ For eruptive rashes with high fever, constipation with hard stools, or mouth and tongue ulcers and swollen painful throat: Mouse-sticky Seed four liang (stir-fried until fragrant), Licorice (honey-fried), Cimicifuga (Shengma), Belamcanda root (Shegan) each one liang. Make into a coarse powder. Each dose three qian, one large cup of water, decoct to six fen, strain and take warm. (Pediatric Smallpox Formulas - Shegan Shuzhanzi Tang)
⒄ For toxic rashes and mumps with swelling and pain: Great Burdock Achene, Bupleurum (Chaihu), Forsythia (Lianqiao), Sichuan Fritillaria (Chuan Beimu), Schizonepeta (Jingjie) each two qian. Decoction and take. (Bencao Huiyan)
⒅ For epidemic pestilence with large-headed swellings: Dali Seed (Dali Zi) and Saposhnikovia (Fangfeng) in equal parts. Grind to powder. Each dose five qian, one large cup of yellow wine, decoct together and take warm on an empty stomach; induce sweating under covers. (Songfeng on Epidemics)

Cultivation and Preparation of Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi)
Source
They are the mature seeds of the leguminous plants Cassia (Jue Ming) and Small Cassia (Xiao Jue Ming). At late autumn when the fruits mature and the pods turn yellow-brown they are harvested by cutting the whole plant and drying, threshing out the seeds, and removing impurities.
Properties and Taste
Salty and bitter; neutral to cool; non-toxic
Preparation
Fried Cassia Seed (Chao Jue Ming Zi): Take clean Cassia seeds, place in a pan and stir-fry until they emit a slight aroma, remove and let cool.
Appearance
(1) Jue Ming (Cassia seed, Jue Ming): Four-angled short cylindrical, one end bluntly rounded, the other end oblique with a point, length 4–6 mm, width 2–3 mm. Surface brown-green or dark brown, smooth and glossy; there is one raised ridge on both dorsal and ventral surfaces; on each side of the ridge there is an oblique light-brown linear groove running from the hilum toward the micropyle. Texture hard. In transverse section the seed coat is thin; endosperm gray-white, semi-translucent; embryo yellow, two cotyledons overlapping and folded in an S-shape. Whole seeds have a slight odor; broken seeds have a faint beany odor; taste slightly bitter and somewhat sticky.
(2) Small Jue Ming (Xiao Jue Ming): Short cylindrical, length 3–5 mm, width 2–2.5 mm. On each side of the ridges there is a broad light yellow-brown band. The best quality has plump grains and a green-brown color.
Effects of Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi)
Efficacy
They are the mature seeds of the leguminous plants Cassia (Jue Ming) and Small Cassia (Xiao Jue Ming).
Main indications: wind-heat red eyes, green blindness, sparrow eye, hypertension, hepatitis, cirrhotic ascites, habitual constipation.
Meridians
Liver Meridian
;
Gallbladder Meridian
;
Kidney Meridian
Indications
Clears the liver, brightens the eyes, promotes diuresis, and relieves constipation. Treats wind-heat red eyes, green blindness, sparrow eye, hypertension, hepatitis, cirrhotic ascites, habitual constipation.
1. Ben Jing: Treats green blindness, ocular discharge with red and white membranes, red painful eyes, lacrimation; long-term use benefits essence and improves vision.
2. Bie Lu: Treats bluish discoloration of the lips and mouth.
3. Yao Xing Lun: Benefits the five viscera and eliminates liver heat.
4. Rihuazi Materia Medica: Aids liver qi, benefits essence and fluids; as a ground powder applied topically it reduces swelling and toxicity; cauterizing the temples treats headache, and applied to the crown stops nasal bleeding; used as a pillow better than black beans, treats head wind and brightens the eyes.
5. Ben Cao Yan Yi Bu Yi: Resolves snake venom.
6. Sheng Cao Yao Xing Bei Yao: Treats pediatric five "gan" disorders and is used to rub ringworm and scabies.
7. Yi Lin Zuan Yao: Drains pathogenic water.
8. Hunan Materia Medica: Brightens the eyes and promotes diuresis. Treats dizziness, beriberi, edema, pulmonary abscess, and chest obstruction.
9. Guangzhou Troops Handbook of Common Chinese Herbs: Clears the liver and brightens the eyes, promotes diuresis and relieves constipation. Treats hepatitis, cirrhotic ascites, hypertension, pediatric malnutrition (gan accumulation), night blindness, wind-heat eye pain, and habitual constipation.
Dosage and Administration
Oral administration: decoction, 9–15 g.
Precautions and Contraindications
Use with caution in cases of diarrhea and low blood pressure. Ben Cao Jing Ji Zhu: Yishi (Achillea seed) serves as its guiding herb; incompatible with hemp seed (Da Ma Zi).
Formulas Containing Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi)
1. For loss of sight, with no other ocular disease and no visual perception, as if seeing through silk: Horseshoe Cassia Seed (Ma Ti Jue Ming) two sheng, pounded and sieved; take with congee one fang-cun spoonful. Avoid fish, garlic, pork, and pungent vegetables. (Seng Shen Ji Fang: Jue Ming San)
2. For red swollen painful eyes: stir-fried Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) ground, mixed with tea, apply to both temples; replace when dry. Also treats hot head-wind headache. (Zhai Yuan Fang)
3. For sparrow eye: Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) 2 liang, Kochia seed (Di Fu Zi) 1 liang. Pound and sieve into a powder. After meals, take one qian mixed with clear congee. (Sheng Hui Fang)
4. To nourish the liver and brighten the eyes: Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) one sheng, Vitex seed (Man Jing Zi) one sheng (soak in good wine five sheng, boil away the wine and sun-dry). Pound and sieve into a powder. Each dose take two qian with warm water, after meals and before bed. (Sheng Hui Fang: Jue Ming Zi San)
5. For acute conjunctivitis: Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) 3 qian, Chrysanthemum flower (Ju Hua) 3 qian, Vitex seed (Man Jing Zi) 2 qian, Horsetail (Mu Zei) 2 qian; decoct in water and take. (Hebei Chinese Materia Medica Handbook)
6. For hypertension: (a) Cassia Seed appropriate amount, fry until yellow, grind into coarse powder, add sugar and soak in boiling water; each dose 3 g, three times daily. (b) Cassia Seed 15 g, Prunella (Xia Ku Cao) 9 g, decoct in water and take continuously for one month. (National Compilation of Chinese Herbs)
7. For pediatric malnutrition accumulation: Grass Cassia Seed (Cao Jue Ming) 9 g, grind to powder; one chicken liver, mash, add a little white wine, mix into a cake, steam until cooked and take. (Jiangxi Herbal Medicine)
8. For chronic ringworm not healing: Cassia Seed ground to fine powder, mix with a small amount of calomel (Qing Fen), rub the lesion to cause slight breakage, then apply the medicine. (Bai Yi Xuan Fang)
9. For long-standing blindness: Cassia Seed two sheng ground to powder; take one spoonful after meals with thin congee.
10. For acute conjunctivitis: Grass Cassia Seed (Cao Jue Ming), Chrysanthemum flower (Ju Hua), Cicada molting (Chan Tui), Celosia seed (Qing Xiang Zi) each 15 g; decoct in water and take. (Qingdao Chinese Herbal Medicine Handbook)
11. For red swollen eyes: stir-fry Cassia Seed, grind fine, mix with tea to a paste and apply to the temples; replace when dry; swelling subsides overnight.
12. For hot head-wind headache: same prescription as above.
13. For nosebleed that will not stop: Cassia Seed three qian ground to powder, add water to make a paste, apply to the chest.
14. For spreading ringworm: Cassia Seed one liang, three qian of powder, add a little mercury and calomel (Qing Fen), grind extremely fine until mercury specks cannot be seen; rub the lesion to break the skin then apply the medicine.
15. For early stage back ulcers: Grass Cassia Seed (raw, Cao Jue Ming) one sheng, pound; raw licorice (Gan Cao) one liang by weight, cut up. Add three sheng of water, boil down to one sheng, warm and divide into two doses. (Pu Ji Fang)
16. For acute keratitis: Cassia Seed 15 g, Chrysanthemum flower 9 g, Gu Jing Cao 9 g, Schizonepeta (Jing Jie) 9 g, Coptis (Huang Lian) 6 g, Akebia (Mu Tong) 12 g; decoct in water and take. (Sichuan Materia Medica, 1979)
17. For night blindness: Cassia Seed and Goji berry (Gou Qi Zi) each 9 g, an appropriate amount of pig liver; decoct, eat the liver and take the soup. (Zhejiang Medicinal Plants)
18. For wind-heat migraine: Cassia Seed and Wild Chrysanthemum (Ye Ju Hua) each 9 g, Ligusticum (Chuan Xiong) 6 g, Vitex seed (Man Jing Zi) 6 g, Whole Scorpion (Quan Xie) 6 g; decoct and take. (Zhejiang Medicinal Plants)
19. For chronic constipation and stubborn post-stroke constipation: Cassia Seed one sheng, stir-fry until aromatic, grind to fine powder, moisten with water and form into pills; take three times daily, one qian each time, continue for 3–5 days until bowel movements are regular and formed without diarrhea; thereafter take a small amount daily to maintain regularity and promote appetite and recovery. (Ben Cao Tui Chen)
20. For habitual constipation: Cassia Seed 18 g, Prunus seed (Yu Li Ren) 18 g; brew with boiling water as a tea. (Anhui Chinese Herbs)
21. For stomatitis: Cassia Seed 60 g; concentrate decoction and frequently gargle. (Anhui Chinese Herbs)
22. For fungal vaginitis: Cassia Seed appropriate amount; decoction used as fumigation and washing for the vulva and vagina. (Zhejiang Medicinal Plants)
Dietary Recipes
1. Grass Cassia Seed and Rabbit Liver Soup
Two rabbit livers, Grass Cassia Seed (Cao Jue Ming) 12 g, a little salt. Put the Grass Cassia Seed into a small cloth bag and together with the rabbit livers place into a pot with clear water and simmer. Season with salt. Drink the soup and eat the rabbit liver with the meal.
Effect: Clears the liver and brightens the eyes, tonifies the middle and benefits qi. Indications: red swollen painful eyes, blurred vision, excessive tearing and other eye disorders.
2. Cassia Seed, Sophora Flower (Huai Hua) and Cattail Pollen (Pu Huang) Tea
Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) 10 g, Sophora flower (Huai Hua) 6 g, Cattail pollen (Pu Huang) 6 g. Put the three ingredients into a thermos, pour boiling water over them, cover and steep for 10 minutes. One dose per day, drink frequently as a tea.
Effect: Lowers blood pressure and blood lipids. Indications: coronary heart disease, hypertension, atherosclerosis, hypercholesterolemia, etc.
3. Double Jue Ming Congee (Shi Jue Ming and Jue Ming Zi)
Shi Jue Ming 25 g, Cassia Seed 10 g, White Chrysanthemum (Bai Ju Hua) 15 g, japonica rice 100 g, rock sugar 6 g. Stir-fry the Cassia Seed until aromatic and remove. Put the white chrysanthemum and Shi Jue Ming into a clay pot and decoct to obtain the juice; strain and discard residues; wash the rice and cook with the medicinal decoction into a thin congee, add rock sugar and eat. Take morning and evening; a course is 3–5 days.
Effect: Nourishes the liver and suppresses rising yang, clears the liver and brightens the eyes. Indicated for red swollen painful eyes, photophobia with excessive tearing, head fullness and headache, or dizziness, blurred vision, and dry eyes due to liver and kidney deficiency or hyperactive liver yang.
4. Chrysanthemum and Cassia Congee
White Chrysanthemum (Bai Ju Hua) and Grass Cassia Seed (Cao Jue Ming) each 10 g, rice 100 g, a little rock sugar. Stir-fry the Grass Cassia Seed until aromatic, decoct with chrysanthemum to obtain the juice, add rice and cook into a thin congee; when cooked add rock sugar and simmer briefly. Take once daily.
This congee can clear the liver, brighten the eyes, lower blood pressure, and can also treat red swollen painful eyes, photophobia with tearing, headache and dizziness, and constipation.
5. Cassia Seed, Cistanche (Rou Cong Rong) and Honey Tea
Stir-fried Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) and Cistanche (Rou Cong Rong) each 10 g, honey to taste. Put both into a teacup, pour boiling water, cover and steep for 10 minutes, add honey to taste. Drink as a tea frequently.
Effect: Moistens the intestines and relieves constipation. Indicated for habitual constipation and senile constipation.
6. Cassia Seed, Nan Sha Shen, Goji and Achyranthes Soup
Cassia Seed 9 g, Nan Sha Shen 15 g, Achyranthes (Niu Xi) 9 g, Goji berry (Gou Qi Zi) 15 g, honey to taste. Put the above four herbs into a pot, decoct, strain and add honey. One dose daily, take for several days.
Effect: Nourishes yin and clears heat, nourishes the liver and brightens the eyes. Indicated for yin-deficient heat-type glaucoma and similar conditions.
7. Hawthorn, Cassia Seed and Lotus Leaf Soup
Hawthorn (Shan Zha) and Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) each 15 g, half a lotus leaf (He Ye). Slice hawthorn, shred lotus leaf, and decoct together with Cassia Seed. Use the decoction as a tea.
Effect: Suitable for coronary heart disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, obesity, etc. Cassia Seed can inhibit increases in serum cholesterol and the formation of aortic atherosclerotic plaques, and its aqueous extract has antihypertensive effects. Lotus leaf quenches thirst, disperses blood stasis, aids the spleen and stomach, and reduces edema. Combined with hawthorn, it can reduce fat and lower blood pressure, promote weight loss and fitness, and is a good medicinal diet for dizziness and vertigo due to hypertension.
8. Cassia Seed, Shepherd's Purse Seed and Celosia Seed Tea
Cassia Seed, Shepherd's purse seed (Ji Cai Zi), and Celosia seed (Qing Xiang Zi) each 6 g. Grind the ingredients to powder, put into a gauze bag, place in a cup and pour boiling water, cover and steep 5–10 minutes. Drink frequently as a tea, one dose per day.
Effect: Clears heat, dispels wind, brightens the eyes, and lowers blood pressure. Indicated for headaches and dizziness in various stages of hypertension.
9. Cassia Seed Congee
Cassia Seed (fried) 10–15 g, japonica rice 100 g, a little rock sugar. First stir-fry the Cassia Seed until aromatic and remove; after it cools put into a clay pot, decoct in water and strain to obtain the decoction; cook the rice with the medicinal decoction and rock sugar into congee. One dose daily; take 5–7 days as a course.
Effect: Clears the liver, brightens the eyes, relieves constipation, lowers blood pressure and blood lipids. Indicated for red swollen painful eyes, photophobia with tearing, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, habitual constipation, etc.
10. Chrysanthemum, Cassia and Prunella Soup
Chrysanthemum flower 12 g, Grass Cassia Seed 30 g, Prunella (Xia Ku Cao) 5 g. Put the three herbs into a pot, decoct in water and strain. One dose daily, take for 5–7 days as a course.
Effect: Clears liver-fire and lowers blood pressure. Indicated for hypertensive headaches and dizziness.

Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E8%BD%A6%E6%A1%91%E5%AD%90%E6%A0%B9
Hopbush root (Che sang zai)
Cultivation and processing of Hopbush root (Che sang zi)
Source
It is the root of the hopbush (po liu), a plant of the Sapindaceae (soapberry) family; it can be harvested year-round and used fresh or sun-dried.
Morphology
Che sang zi (the hopbush) is a shrub or small tree, 1–3 m or taller; young branches flattened, with narrow wings or angles, covered with a glutinous mucilage. Leaves simple, alternate; petiole short or nearly sessile; leaf blade papery, shape and size highly variable, linear, linear-spatulate, linear-lanceolate, ob-lanceolate or oblong, 5–12 cm long, 0.5–4 cm wide, apex shortly acuminate, obtuse or rounded, margin entire or with indistinct shallow undulations, both surfaces sticky, glabrous, shiny when dry. Flowers solitary in axils, plant dioecious; inflorescences terminal or axillary on upper parts of branches, shorter than leaves, densely flowered, with angled rachis and branches; pedicels slender, 2–5 mm long, sometimes up to 1 cm; calyx 4, lanceolate or oblong-lanceolate, about 3 mm long, apex obtuse; stamens 7 or 8, filaments under 1 mm, anthers 2.5 mm long, incurved, with glandular points; ovary ovoid, externally covered with a glutinous mucilage, 2- or 3-locular, style about 6 mm long, apex deeply 2- or 3-cleft. Capsule inversely heart-shaped or depressed globose, 2- or 3-winged, wings 1.8–2.5 cm wide, seed coat membranous or papery with veins. Seeds 1 or 2 per locule, lens-shaped, black. Flowering in late autumn, fruiting from late winter to early spring.
Habitat and distribution
Ecological environment: grows on dry hillsides, open ground or sandy soils by the sea.
Resource distribution: distributed in the southeastern, southern to southwestern regions of China.
Taste and properties
Taste bitter; nature cold
Effects of Hopbush root (Che sang zi)
Efficacy
It is the root of the hopbush (po liu) of the Sapindaceae family; mainly used for toothache and wind-toxin streaming conditions.
Indications
Drains fire and detoxifies. Mainly for toothache and wind-toxin streaming down.
Dosage and administration
Internal use: decoction, 15–30 g; fresh material 30–60 g.
Formulas containing Hopbush root (Che sang zi)
1. For toothache: one to two liang of fresh Che sang zai root. Decoction with water for oral administration.
2. For wind-toxin streaming down: one to two liang of dried Che sang zai root, stewed together with an appropriate amount of lean pork and taken as a broth; additionally mash fresh leaves with brown sugar and apply the paste to the affected area.

Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E6%A8%B1%E6%A1%83%E6%A0%B8
Name
Cherry seed (Yingtao mi)
Cherry seed (Yingtao mi)
Cultivation and processing of Cherry kernel (Yingtao he)
Source
This item is the dried mature fruit stone of Cherry (Yingtao) of the Rosaceae family. In summer, mature fruits are placed in a jar and rubbed with implements to separate the flesh from the stones; the flesh is then washed away, the clean stones are taken and sun-dried.
[Morphology]
Cherry (Yingtao) is a deciduous shrub or tree, 3–8 m tall. Bark gray-white with obvious lenticels; young shoots glabrous or with sparse soft hairs. Leaves alternate; petiole 0.7–1.5 cm long, with sparse soft hairs, apex with one or two large glands; stipules lanceolate, with pinnatifid glandular teeth, early deciduous; leaf blade ovate or oblong-ovate, 5–12 cm long, 3–5 cm wide, apex gradually acuminate or caudate-acuminate, base rounded, margin with sharp coarse serrations, tooth apices with small glands, adaxial surface dark green and nearly glabrous, abaxial surface pale green with sparse soft hairs along veins or between veins; flowers bisexual, inflorescences umbel-like or nearly umbellate; 3–6 flowers, opening before the leaves; pedicel 8–19 mm long, with sparse soft hairs; hypanthium campanulate, externally with sparse soft hairs; calyx lobes 5, triangular-ovate or ovate-lanceolate; apex acute or obtuse; petals 5, white, obovate, apex concave or bifid; stamens 30–35, up to 50 in cultivation; style nearly as long as stamens, glabrous; pistil 1, ovary inferior. Drupe nearly globose, red, 9–13 mm in diameter, one seed enclosed in a yellowish-white woody endocarp. Flowering period March–April. Fruiting period May–June.
Characteristics
This item is flat-ovoid or oblong-ovoid, length 0.6–0.9 cm, 0.7–1 cm, diameter 0.5–0.7 cm. Surface pale yellow to gray-yellow, with slightly raised reticulate texture; one end pointed, slightly beak-like, the other end with an oblong pit; dorsal suture line slightly prominent, ventral suture line distinctly prominent, each side with a longitudinal raised rib, edge with a ridge line. Texture hard. When broken, one seed is visible, flat-ovoid, yellow-brown, surface with fine wrinkles. Seed coat thin, two cotyledons, pale yellow, rich in oil. Smell slight, taste slightly bitter.
[Nature, Taste, and Meridian Affinities]
Pungent, neutral in nature. Enters the Lung channel.
[Functions and Indications]
Disperses and promotes the eruption of rashes; detoxifies. Indicated for early-stage measles with incomplete eruption.
[Usage and Dosage]
Internal use: decocted as a decoction, 4.5–9 g, crushed at time of use.
External use: apply the pressed juice topically or use the decoction to wash.
Effects of Cherry kernel (Yingtao he)
Efficacy
This item is the dried mature fruit stone of Cherry (Yingtao) of the Rosaceae family. Indicated for early-stage measles with incomplete eruption.
Precautions and Contraindications
Illustrated Materia Medica of Southern Yunnan: avoid in yang-type pox conditions.
Prescriptions using Cherry kernel (Yingtao he)
1. For treating hoarseness after pox eruption: Sweet cherry kernels (Tian yingtao he), twenty pieces. Roast in an earthenware pot until yellow, decoct and drink. (Supplement to the Compendium of Materia Medica)
2. For treating eyelid tumors: grind Cherry kernels (Yingtao he) with water and apply the paste; the tumor gradually disappears. (Medical Guide)

Source: https://zhongyibaike.com/wiki/%E7%B2%89%E8%8B%9E%E8%8B%A3
Name
Herb of Slender-leaf Ixeris (fen bao ju)
Slender-leaf Bitter-herb (xi ye ku cai)
Slender-leaf Bitter-herb (xi ye ku cai)
Slender-leaf Ixeris (xi ye ku mai)
Cultivation and Processing of Slender-leaf Ixeris (fen bao ju)
Source
From the whole herb of the Asteraceae plant Slender-leaf Ixeris (xi ye ku mai). Harvested in July to August, washed clean, sun-dried or used fresh.
Original morphology
Slender-leaf Ixeris (xi ye ku mai), a herbaceous plant, 16–50 cm tall. The whole plant is slender. The entire plant is glabrous. Basal leaves in a rosette, linear-lanceolate, 7–15 cm long, 5–9 mm wide, apex gradually acute, base narrowed into a short petiole, margins entire, sometimes ciliate near the base of the margin; upper stem leaves similar to basal leaves but smaller and sessile. Capitula numerous, arranged in corymb-like clusters, with slender peduncles; involucre 5–7 mm long; outer involucral bracts ovate, inner involucral bracts 7–8, linear, apex slightly obtuse; ligulate florets yellow, 7–9 mm long, apex 5-toothed. Achenes fusiform, slightly flattened, brownish, about 3 mm long, with longitudinal ribs, beak short about 1 mm long, pappus light brown, 3–4 mm long.
Habitat and Distribution
Ecology: grows by roadsides, grassy slopes and wastelands.
Resource distribution: distributed in Central China, South China and Pei.
Nature and Taste
Taste: bitter; Nature: slightly cold
Characteristics
Whole herb 10–30 cm long. Stem single or branched at the base. Leaves alternate, folded; when flattened the intact leaves are linear-lanceolate or long linear, 4–15 cm long, 5–9 mm wide, margins entire, nearly sessile. Capitula arranged in corymbiform clusters. Achenes fusiform, brownish, with longitudinal ribs, beak short about 1 mm long. Smell faint, taste bitter.
Effects of Slender-leaf Ixeris (fen bao ju)
Efficacy
From the whole herb of the Asteraceae plant Slender-leaf Ixeris (xi ye ku mai). Main indications: jaundice-type hepatitis, conjunctivitis, and boils.
Indications
Clears heat and detoxifies, relieves pain. Used for jaundice-type hepatitis, conjunctivitis, and boils.
1. "Commonly Used Tibetan Medicinal Herbs": clears heat and detoxifies, anti-inflammatory and analgesic. Treats jaundice-type hepatitis, conjunctivitis, and boils.
2. "Flora of Guangxi": treats cough and skin ulcers/sores.
Usage and Dosage
Internal use: decoction, 6–12 g.
External use: appropriate amount, pounded and applied as a poultice.

Cultivation and Processing of Chrysanthemum (Ju Hua)
Source
The capitulum (head inflorescence) of Chrysanthemum, a plant of the Asteraceae family. Harvest when flowers are in full bloom before the first frost; processing methods vary by producing area and material type.
White chrysanthemum (Bai Ju): cut flower-bearing branches, tie into small bunches, hang upside down to dry in the shade. Then pick off the flower heads.
Chu chrysanthemum (Chu Ju): pick off the flower heads. Sulfur-fumigate; when sun-dried to about sixty percent dry, sieve into ball shapes and sun-dry.
Tribute chrysanthemum (Gong Ju): pick off the flower heads and dry by baking.
Hang chrysanthemum (Hang Ju): includes Hang white chrysanthemum and Hang yellow chrysanthemum; Hang white chrysanthemum: pick off the flower heads, steam and then sun-dry; Hang yellow chrysanthemum: dry with charcoal heat.
Properties and Flavor
Taste: sweet; bitter; nature: slightly cold
Appearance and Characteristics
(1) Hairy chrysanthemum (Hao Ju)
Capitula conical-obtuse or cylindrical, sometimes slightly compressed and lobed, diameter 1.5–3 cm. Involucre discoid, with 3–4 layers of involucre bracts, ovate to elliptic, herbaceous, yellow-green or brown-green, externally with soft hairs, membranous margin; receptacle hemispherical, without receptacular bracts or receptacle hairs. Ray florets several rows, female, located at the periphery, colored off-white, erect, stiff, longitudinally folded and contracted, scattered with golden glandular dots; disc florets numerous, bisexual, located centrally and concealed by ray florets, yellow, apex 5-toothed. Achenes undeveloped, without pappus. Light in weight, soft and moist in texture, brittle when dry. Fragrant aroma, taste sweet and slightly bitter.
(2) Chu chrysanthemum (Chu Ju)
Irregular globose or depressed-globose, diameter 1.5–2.5 cm. Ray florets white, irregularly twisted, involute, margins wrinkled, sometimes with light brown glandular dots; disc florets mostly concealed.
(3) Tribute chrysanthemum (Gong Ju)
Depressed-globose or irregular globose, diameter 1.5–2.5 cm. Ray florets white or off-white, ascending obliquely, some reflexed, margins slightly involute and wrinkled, usually without glandular dots; few disc florets exposed.
(4) Hang chrysanthemum (Hang Ju)
Disc-shaped or depressed-globose, diameter 2.5–4 cm, often several connected into clusters. Ray florets generally white or yellow, flat or slightly folded, often adherent to each other and often without glandular dots; disc florets numerous and exposed. Best quality is when flowers are intact without scattered petals, color white (or yellow), strong fragrance, and free of impurities.
Actions of Chrysanthemum
Efficacy
The capitulum of Chrysanthemum, a plant of the Asteraceae family.
Indications
For headache, dizziness, red eyes, vexation and heat in the chest, sores and abscesses, swellings and toxin.
Channels Entered
Enters the Lung meridian; Liver meridian
Main Uses
Dispels wind, clears heat, brightens the eyes, detoxifies. Treats headache, dizziness, red eyes, vexation and heat in the chest, sores, and swellings with toxin.
1. Ben Jing (Classic Materia Medica): Treats various wind-induced dizziness, swelling and pain, eyes feeling as if dislodged with tearing, skin necrosis and muscle death, aversion to wind and damp painful obstruction, benefits blood and qi.
2. Bie Lu (Supplemental Records): Heals wandering low back pain, removes vexation and heat in the chest, calms the stomach and intestines, benefits the five vessels, and regulates the four limbs.
3. Tao Hongjing: White chrysanthemum (Bai Ju): treats wind-induced vertigo.
4. Yao Xing Lun (Treatise on Medicinal Properties): Can treat hot wind causing vertigo and collapse, pain of brain and bones, and disperses various forms of wind affecting the body.
5. Ri Hua Zi Ben Cao (Daily Flower Materia Medica): Benefits the blood vessels, treats wandering wind of the limbs, vexation, oppression in the chest and diaphragm, as well as sores and toxins and headaches; used as a pillow to brighten the eyes.
6. Zhen Zhu Nang (Pearl Pouch): Nourishes the blood of the eyes.
7. Yong Yao Xin Fa (Essentials of Drug Use): Removes ocular film and brightens the eyes.
8. Wang Haogu: Treats liver qi deficiency.
9. Gang Mu Shi Yi (Supplement to the Compendium): Specifically enters the yang aspect. Treats wind-induced dizziness and relieves alcohol toxin and sores and swellings. Yellow tea chrysanthemum: brightens the eyes and dispels wind, pacifies liver qi, treats dizziness and blurred vision, nourishes blood and moistens the complexion, enters the blood level; white tea chrysanthemum: unblocks lung qi, stops rebellious cough, clears heat in the triple burner, treats muscular heat, enters the qi level.
Dosage and Administration
Internal use: decoction 10–15 g; or used in pills or powders; or steeped as tea.
External use: appropriate amount, decocted water for washing; or pounded into a poultice.
Precautions and Contraindications
Ben Cao Hui Yan (Materia Medica Notes): In cases of qi deficiency and cold stomach, poor appetite, and diarrhea, use sparingly. Contraindicated in yang deficiency or headache with aversion to cold.
Prescriptions Using Chrysanthemum
1. For wind-heat headache: Chrysanthemum (Ju Hua), Gypsum (Shi Gao), Chuanxiong (Chuan Xiong) each 3 qian. Grind to powder. Each dose 1.5 qian, taken with tea. (Simple Single Formula)
2. For Taiyin wind-warmth with cough, slight fever, and mild thirst: Bitter Apricot Kernel (Ku Xing Ren) 2 qian, Forsythia (Lian Qiao) 1.5 qian, Mint (Bo He) 8 fen, Mulberry Leaf (Sang Ye) 2.5 qian, Chrysanthemum (Ju Hua) 1 qian, Bitter Platycodon Root (Ku Jie Geng) 2 qian, Licorice (Gan Cao) 8 fen, Reed Root (Lu Gen) 2 qian. Two cups of water, decoct down to one cup, take three times daily. (Wen Bing Tiao Bian — Mulberry-Chrysanthemum Drink)
3. For wind-induced vertigo: Sweet chrysanthemum flowers dried rapidly. Make into powder, wrap in rice as offering and steam to make wine for drinking. (Xu Sibo — Chrysanthemum Wine)
4. For hot-toxin wind attacking upwards with red eyes, dizzy head, blurred vision and facial swelling: Baked Chrysanthemum (Ju Hua, baked), Baked Paifengzi (Pai Feng Zi, baked), Processed Licorice (Gan Cao, processed) each 1 liang. Pound the three ingredients and sieve into a powder. At bedtime take 3 qian dissolved in warm water. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu — Chrysanthemum Powder)
5. For various eye obscurations and dimness: Sichuan pepper (Shu Jiao, remove seeds and close the mouth, fry to sweat, 1.5 jin, pound and sieve to a powder) 1 jin, Sweet Chrysanthemum Flower (baked and powdered) 1 jin. Mix the two powders evenly with 15 jin of fat Rehmannia (prepared Di Huang) sliced and pounded, press and collect about 8–9 dou of juice, mix the earlier powdered herbs into the juice until even, sun-dry slightly until not too dry, place in a pan and sun-dry for three to four days until dry but not over-dried, then add 2 jin refined honey and pound thousands of times into pills the size of a catalpa seed. Each dose 30 pills, taken on an empty stomach at noon with warm water. (Sheng Ji Zong Lu — Night Brightening Pills)
6. For liver and kidney deficiency with virtual fire flaring upwards, red painful swollen eyes, long-term blurred vision, tearing in wind, photophobia, dizziness, night sweats, tidal fever, and weakness of the feet: Goji Berry (Gou Qi Zi), Sweet Chrysanthemum Flower (Ju Hua), Prepared Rehmannia Root (Shu Di Huang), Cornus (Shan Zhu Yu), Prepared Chinese Yam (Huai Shan Yao), Poria (Bai Fu Ling), Moutan Bark (Mu Dan Pi), Alisma (Ze Xie). Refined honey made into pills. (Yi Ji — Qi Ju Di Huang Wan)
7. For liver and kidney deficiency and blurred vision: Sweet Chrysanthemum Flower 4 liang, Morinda Root (Ba Ji Tian, remove central core) 1 liang, Cistanche (Rou Cong Rong, wine-soaked, peeled, fried, sliced and baked) 2 liang, Goji Berry 3 liang. Grind to fine powder, make pills with refined honey the size of a catalpa seed. Each dose 30–50 pills, taken with warm wine or salted broth on an empty stomach before meals. (Ju Jing Wan — Chrysanthemum and Jing Pill)
8. For post-illness ocular film: White Chrysanthemum (Bai Ju Hua) and Cicada Molting (Chan Tui) equal parts; make into powder. Each use 2–3 qian with a little honey, decoct in water and take. (Jiu Ji Fang — Emergency Prescriptions)
9. For carbuncles: White Chrysanthemum 4 liang, Licorice (Gan Cao) 4 qian. Decoct in water and take immediately; decoct the residue again and take. (Wai Ke Shi Fa — Chrysanthemum and Licorice Decoction)
10. For knee wind (rheumatic knee pain): Aged Mugwort (Ai Ye), Chrysanthemum. Make into a knee pad and use for a long time. (Fu Shou Jing Fang)
11. For unilateral or bilateral headache: Sweet Chrysanthemum Flower, Gypsum (Shi Gao), Chuanxiong (Chuan Xiong) each 3 qian. Grind to powder. Each dose 3 qian, taken with clear tea. (Wei Sheng Yi Jian Fang)
12. For red swollen painful eyes: Tea chrysanthemum 15 g, Tribulus (Bai Ci Li) 15 g, Horsetail (Mu Zei) 15 g, Cicada Molting (Chan Tui) 6 g. Decoction in water and take. (Sichuan Materia Medica, 1982 edition)
13. For hypertension: White chrysanthemum 15 g, three red dates. Decoction in water and take. (Fujian Materia Medica)
14. For low back pain: Chrysanthemum 2 sheng, Daphne (Yuan Hua) 2 sheng, Azalea (Yang Zhi Zhu) 2 sheng. Mix the three with vinegar until damp, divide into two doses, place in a cloth bag and steam like cooking about one dou of rice; when warm, apply as a compress, reheat when cold, and pain will resolve. (Wai Tai)
15. For itchy yin sores: Chrysanthemum, pomegranate root bark; decoct and use for steam washing. (Pu Ji Fang)
16. For carbuncles: Chrysanthemum with stems pounded for juice and mixed with warm wine to take orally, use the residue as topical poultice for immediate effect. (Ping Xi Dan Fang Xuan)
17. For common warts: Chrysanthemum 30 g, 100 ml 30-degree baijiu (white liquor) (if baijiu is too strong, dilute with boiled water to 30 degrees). Place chrysanthemum in the baijiu and soak for 3 days, then discard residue; add appropriate amount of boiled water to the infusion and simmer with white sugar to take once daily; one course is 3 days, stop and observe for 3 days; if ineffective, take a second course, up to 5 consecutive courses. (Fujian Traditional Chinese Medicine, 1985, (1):63)
18. For drinking without getting drunk: On the ninth day of the ninth lunar month take a pinch of chrysanthemum powder immediately before drinking. (Qian Jin Yao Fang)
Dietary Therapy Recipes
1. Egg and Chrysanthemum Soup
One egg, Chrysanthemum 5 g, lotus root juice appropriate amount, a little mature vinegar. Mix beaten egg with chrysanthemum, lotus root juice and vinegar, steam over water until cooked; take once daily.
Efficacy: Hemostatic and promoting blood circulation, reduces swelling and relieves pain. Suitable for advanced esophageal cancer with increased coughing and marked vomiting.
2. Safflower, Mulberry Leaf and Chrysanthemum Soup
Safflower (Hong Hua) 3 g, Mulberry Leaf (Sang Ye) 10 g, Chrysanthemum (Ju Hua) 10 g. Place mulberry leaves, chrysanthemum and safflower in a cup, pour boiling water, cover and steep briefly; first use the vapor to fumigate the affected eye, then drink warm. Twice daily for three consecutive days.
Efficacy: Disperses heat and reduces swelling, relieves pain and brightens the eyes. Indicated for acute infective conjunctivitis and related conditions.
3. Chrysanthemum and Licorice Decoction
White chrysanthemum (or chrysanthemum) 120 g, Licorice (Gan Cao) 12 g. Add water and decoct, divide into 3–4 doses.
Efficacy: Clears heat and detoxifies. Indicated for sores and swollen painful abscesses.
4. Mulberry, Chrysanthemum and Cicada-Shell Drink
Mulberry Leaf 10 g, Chrysanthemum 10 g, Cicada Molting (Chan Tui) 6 g, sugar to taste. Clean mulberry leaves and chrysanthemum, remove head and feet of cicada molting, place together in a pot with appropriate water, bring to a boil over high heat then simmer over low heat for 15 minutes, strain and collect the decoction, add sugar and stir. Drink regularly.
Efficacy: Releases exterior wind-heat and calms convulsions. Indicated for pediatric convulsions with fever, headache, cough and rhinorrhea.
5. Chrysanthemum and Oolong Tea
Hang Chrysanthemum 10 g, Oolong tea 3 g, pour boiling water to steep as tea.
Efficacy: Pacifies the liver, dispels wind-heat, generates fluids and relieves thirst, diuretic, can lower serum cholesterol and help prevent atherosclerosis. Suitable for hypertension due to liver-yang rising and yin deficiency with relative yang excess.
6. Chrysanthemum and Reed-Root Tea
Chrysanthemum 10 g, Reed Root (Lu Gen) 60 g. Wash and chop reed root, decoct together with chrysanthemum, strain and drink as tea.
Efficacy: Clears lung heat, promotes urination and brings out rashes. Indicated for pediatric measles and chickenpox.
7. Chrysanthemum Congee
Chrysanthemum (ground to powder) and polished rice in a ratio of 1:2. Cook rice into congee, when nearly done add chrysanthemum powder (amount one), then bring to a boil and serve twice daily warm. Contraindicated for spleen deficiency with loose stools.
Efficacy: For red swollen painful eyes, blurred vision, hypertension, dilation of coronary arteries and increased coronary blood flow.
8. Chrysanthemum, Cassia Seed and Prunella Decoction
Chrysanthemum 12 g, Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) 30 g, Prunella (Xia Ku Cao) 5 g. Put the three herbs in a pot, decoct, strain and take the decoction. One dose daily, use for 5–7 days per course.
Efficacy: Clears liver-fire and lowers blood pressure. Indicated for hypertension with headache and dizziness.
9. Chrysanthemum, Mulberry, Mint and Bamboo-Leaf Tea
Chrysanthemum 5 g, Mulberry Leaf 5 g, Mint 3 g, Bamboo Leaf (Dan Zhu Ye) 30 g, White Imperata Root (Bai Mao Gen) 30 g. Put all ingredients into a teapot, pour boiling water and steep for 10 minutes. Drink as a beverage as desired.
Efficacy: Acrid-cool to release exterior, clears and benefits the throat. Indicated for wind-heat common cold with fever, headache, spontaneous sweating, nasal congestion, sore throat and productive cough with thick phlegm.
10. Chrysanthemum Tea
Tea leaves 3 g, dried chrysanthemum 5–10 g, pour boiling water to steep and drink after meals.
Efficacy: Reduces fever and detoxifies, clears the liver and brightens the eyes, lowers lipids and has anti-aging effects. Drinking chrysanthemum with Longjing tea may also treat mild hypertension, conjunctivitis and dizziness from diminished vision.
11. Chrysanthemum and Cassia Seed Congee
Take Chrysanthemum and Cassia Seed (Jue Ming Zi) each 10 g, rice 100 g, rock sugar to taste. Roast Cassia Seed until fragrant, decoct together with chrysanthemum to obtain a strained juice, add rice and cook into thin congee, when cooked add rock sugar and simmer briefly. Take once daily.
Efficacy: Clears the liver, brightens the eyes and lowers blood pressure; can also treat red swollen painful eyes, photophobia with tearing, headache and dizziness, and constipation.
12. Two-Flower Tea
Honeysuckle (Jin Yin Hua) 50 g, Hang chrysanthemum 100 g, honey to taste. Remove impurities, wash and briefly pan-fry, cool and store in a clean jar. When needed take a small amount, place in a cup, pour boiling water and steep, add honey to taste. Take 2–3 times daily.
Efficacy: Clears heat and dispels wind, brightens the eyes and lowers blood pressure. Indicated for summer heat thirst, hypertension, coronary heart disease, palpitations and insomnia, sore throat and cough. Also suitable as a cooling summer beverage.

Cultivation and processing of Cicada Slough
Source
This material is the shed exoskeleton of the larvae of the cicada Cryptotympana pustulata Fabricius (family Cicadidae) after molting. Collected in summer and autumn, remove dirt and sand, sun-dry.
Properties (taste and nature)
Flavor: sweet; salty; Nature: cold
Processing
Boji Fang: remove earth, claws, face; wash clean and use.
Xiao Er Yao Zheng Zhi Jue: remove head, feet, and dirt; wash with water, sun-dry, grind to powder, use with water flying three times.
Paozhi Dafa: wash with boiling water to remove soil, remove head, wings and feet and use. Current practice: take the raw material, remove impurities, wash clean, dry.
Characteristics
Whole form resembles a cicada and is hollow, slightly curved. Length about 3–4 centimeters, width about 1.5–2 centimeters. Surface is tea-brown, semi-translucent, glossy, covered with fine black-brown or yellow-brown hairs. Head has one pair of antennae, filiform, often broken off; compound eyes protruding, transparent; forehead protruding; labrum short and broad, labium elongate into a tube. Dorsal thorax longitudinally split or split crosswise in a cruciform manner; left and right each have two pairs of small wings, the anterior pair longer, the posterior pair shorter; ventrally three pairs of legs, foreleg femur and tibia with serrations at the tips, foreleg tarsi with two small spines at tips, teeth and spines are black-brown; midlegs and hindlegs are slender and long. Abdomen flattened and rounded; divided into nine segments, tail end triangular and bluntly pointed. Body light, membranous, hollow, brittle. Smell weak, taste mild. The best are those yellow in color, light in weight, intact, and free of dirt and sand.
Effects of Cicada Slough
Functions
This material is the shed exoskeleton of the larvae of the cicada species Cryptotympana pustulata.
Main indications: external-contracted wind-heat, cough with hoarseness, measles failing to surface, urticarial itching, pediatric convulsions, eye redness, eye opacities, carbuncles and toxic swellings, tetanus.
Meridians
Lung meridian; Liver meridian
Indications
Disperse wind-heat, release the lungs, and stop spasms. Treats externally contracted wind-heat, cough with hoarseness, measles failing to surface, urticarial itching, pediatric convulsions, eye redness, eye opacities, carbuncles and toxic swellings, tetanus.
① Bie Lu: treats pediatric convulsions; ashes applied cure chronic dysentery.
② Yao Xing Lun: treats children with whole-body feverish convulsions and also quenches thirst.
③ Ben Cao Shi Yi: grind one qian spoon, take with well water, treats aphonia.
④ Ben Cao Yan Yi: treats blurred vision and eye opacities. Also decoct the shell to obtain juice, treats children with delayed eruption of rashes and discomfort.
⑤ Ben Cao Gang Mu: treats wind in the head causing vertigo, skin wind-heat, itchy smallpox eruptions, tetanus and treatment of swelling-toxin sores, adult loss of voice, pediatric trismus and upward-gazing spasms, fright-induced crying and night crying, genital swellings.
Dosage and administration
Internal use: decoct as a decoction, 3–6 g; or enter into pills or powders.
External use: appropriate amount, decocted water for washing; or grind to powder and apply as a paste.
Precautions and contraindications
Use with caution during pregnancy.
Formulas containing Cicada Slough
① For early-stage wind-warmth, newly contracted wind-heat, winter-warm invading the lung, cough: Mint (Bohe) 1 qian 5 fen, Cicada Slough (Chantui) 1 qian (remove feet and wings), Peucedanum Root (Qianhu) 1 qian 5 fen, Fermented Soybeans (Dandouchi) 4 qian, Trichosanthes Peel (Gualoupi) 2 qian, Burdock Seed (Niubangzi) 1 qian 5 fen. Decoction and take. (Shi Bing Lun, method of acrid-cool release of the exterior)
② For cough with obstructed lung qi: Cicada shell (Chanke, remove earth, lightly stir-fry), Ginseng (Renshen, remove fibrous root), Schisandra (Wuweizi) one liang each, Tangerine Peel (Chenpi), Licorice (Gancao, honey-fried) each half liang. Grind to fine powder. Each dose half qian, take with fresh ginger soup, no fixed time. (Xiao Er Wei Sheng Zong Wei Lun Fang, Cicada Shell Decoction)
③ For common cold with cough and loss of voice: Cicada garment (Chanyi) 1 qian, Burdock Seed (Niubangzi) 3 qian, Licorice (Gancao) 1 qian, Platycodon Root (Jiegeng) 1 qian 5 fen. Decoction and take. (Modern Practical Chinese Medicine)
④ For incompletely erupting smallpox: Lithospermum Root (Zicao), Cicada Slough (Chantui), Akebia Stem (Mutong), Peony (Bai Shao), Licorice (Gancao, honey-fried) equal parts. Each dose 2 qian, decoct and take. (Xiao Er Dou Zhen Fang Lun, Kuai Tou San)
⑤ For wind-invaded skin causing persistent itching: Cicada Slough (Chantui) and Mint leaves (Bohe Ye) equal parts. Grind to powder. Mix with wine to 1 qian spoon, take three times daily. (Yao Seng Tan Ji Yan Fang)
⑥ For post-smallpox fever and itching with scratching-induced lesions: Cicada retreat (Chantui) and Lycii Cortex (Digupi) each 1 liang. Grind to powder. Each dose 2–3 spoonfuls, take with white wine two to three times. (Chi Shui Xuan Zhu, Chantui Powder)
⑦ For convulsions with high fever and spasms: Cicada shell (Chanke, remove soil, stir-fry) 0.5 liang, Ginseng (Renshen, remove fibrous root) 0.5 liang, Scutellaria (Huangqin) 1 fen, Poria (Fushen) 1 fen, Cimicifuga (Shengma) 1 fen, grind the above to fine powder; Bovine gallstone (Niuhuang) 1 fen (male ground), Bamboo bezoar (Tianzhu Huang) 1 qian (ground), Oyster shell (Muli) 1 fen (ground). Mix evenly and finely; each dose half qian, decoct with Schizonepeta (Jingjie) and Mint (Bohe) soup and take as needed. (Xiao Er Wei Sheng Zong Wei Lun Fang, Cicada Shell Powder)
⑧ For pediatric upward-gazing spasm, head and eyes turned upward, phlegm blocking internal heat: Jinniuer, boil in slurry water for one day, sun-dry and grind to powder, each dose one character (a traditional small measure), take with cold water. (Wei Sheng Yi Jian Fang)
⑨ For pediatric trismus at birth with inability to suckle: Cicada Slough 27 pieces, Whole Scorpion (Quan Xie) 27 pieces. Grind to powder, add a small amount of Litargirio (Qingfen) powder, mix with breast milk and feed. (Quan You Xin Jian)
⑩ For pediatric night crying: Cicada retreat 27 pieces, Cinnabar (Zhusha) a small amount. Grind to powder, make honey pills, let the child suck. (Chi Shui Xuan Zhu, Chantui Paste)
(11) For tetanus: Cicada Slough (remove earth) any amount. Grind to fine powder. Sprinkle into the wound; the toxic qi will disperse. (Yang family household prescriptions, Zhui Feng Powder)
(12) For scrofulous sores affecting the eye or post-illness eye opacities: Cicada Slough (wash clean, remove earth) and White Chrysanthemum Flower (Juhua) equal parts. Each dose 2 qian, one cup of water, add a little honey, decoct and take after milk feeding, adjust dose by child size. (Xiao Er Dou Zhen Fang Lun, Cicada-Chrysanthemum Powder)
(13) For internal eye opacities: Dragon shed (that is Snake Slough), Cicada retreat, Fenghuang retreat (that is eggshell of ornamental fowl), Human shed (Ren Tui), Buddha slough (that is silkworm shed). Equal parts, do not measure quantitatively, burn together to ash, grind to fine powder. Each dose 1 qian, eat with hot pig liver, any time, three times daily. (Ophthalmology Long Mu Lun, Five Retreats Powder)
(14) For treating sores: Cicada retreat shell and White Stiff Silkworm (Baijiangcan) equal parts. Grind to powder, mix with vinegar and apply around the lesion, leaving the ulcer opening, wait until the root emerges somewhat long, then extract the root and then apply medicine to the sore. Another formula uses oil instead of vinegar for mixing and applying. (Sheng Hui Fang, Cicada Slough Powder)
(15) For scrofula: open a walnut, remove half the kernel, fill the cavity with Cicada Slough, seal externally with yellow loam, tie with iron wire, roast over low heat until dry and the mud falls off, then grind the walnut finely, take with yellow wine as an adjuvant, mix with hot water and drink, take one walnut on an empty stomach each morning, continue for one hundred days. (Hebei Traditional Chinese Medicine Collection)
(16) For otitis with pus discharge: Cicada Slough half a liang (heat-treated to retain activity), Musk (Shexiang) half qian (stir-fried), grind to powder, wrap in cotton and plug, expel the foul matter. (Hai Shang Fang)
(17) For pediatric genital swelling: Cicada Slough half a liang, decoct to wash; also give Wuling Powder internally, then the swelling subsides and pain stops. (Shi Yi De Xiao Fang)
Dietary therapy formula
Mulberry-Chrysanthemum-Cicada Slough Drink (Sang Ju Chantui Yin)
Mulberry Leaf (Sangye) 10 g, Chrysanthemum Flower (Juhua) 10 g, Cicada Garment (Chanyi) 6 g, White Sugar appropriate amount. Select and clean mulberry leaves and chrysanthemum flowers, remove head and feet of cicada garment, place all into a pot, add appropriate amount of water, bring to a boil over high heat, then simmer over low heat for 15 minutes, strain to obtain decoction. Add white sugar and stir to dissolve. Drink regularly.
Functions: dispel wind and clear heat, calm convulsions. Indications: pediatric convulsions with fever, headache, cough, runny nose, etc.
